Tischler and Piet Maes The citation for this ICTV Report chapter is the summary published as: Bradfute, S. B., Calisher, C. H., Klempa, B., Klingström, J., Kuhn, J. H., Laenen, L., Tischler, N. D., & Maes, P. (2024). ICTV Virus Taxonomy Profile: Hantaviridae 2024, Journal of General Virology 105, 001975 Corresponding author: Piet Maes ( [email protected] ) Edited by: Holly Hughes and Evelien Adriaenssens Posted: March 2024, updated June 2024 Summary Hantaviridae is a family for negative-sense RNA viruses with genomes of about 10.5–14.6 kb (Table 1 Hantaviridae ). The family includes eight genera ( Actinovirus and Percilovirus (subfamily Actantavirinae ), Agnathovirus (subfamily Agantavirinae ), Loanvirus , Mobatvirus , Orthohantavirus and Thottimvirus (subfamily Mammantavirinae ), and Reptillovirus (subfamily Repantavirinae ). These viruses are maintained in and/or transmitted by small mammals, but also by fish and reptiles. Several orthohantaviruses can infect humans, causing mild, severe, and sometimes-fatal diseases. Hantavirids produce enveloped virions containing three single-stranded RNA segments with open reading frames (ORFs) that encode a nucleoprotein (N), a glycoprotein precursor (GPC), and large (L) protein containing an RNA-directed RNA polymerase (RdRP) domain. Table 1 Hantaviridae. Characteristics of members of the family Hantaviridae. Characteristic Description* Example Hantaan virus (S segment: M14626; M segment: M14627; L segment: X55901), species Orthohantavirus hantanense Virion Enveloped, pleomorphic virions 80–160 nm in diameter with heterodimeric surface spikes Genome Three single-stranded RNA molecules (segments): small (S; 1.0–3.0 kb), medium (M; 3.4–4.8 kb), and large (L; 5.3–6.8 kb) Replication Ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes containing anti-genomic RNA serve as coding templates for synthesis of genomic RNA Translation Proteins are produced from capped and non-polyadenylated mRNAs. The 5′-cap structure is obtained via cap-snatching from cellular mRNAs Host range Fish (actinoviruses, agnathoviruses, perciloviruses), mammals (orthohantaviruses), and reptiles (reptilloviruses) Taxonomy Realm Riboviria , kingdom Orthornavirae , phylum Negarnaviricota , class Bunyaviricetes , order Elliovirales ; the family includes four subfamilies, eight genera, and 55 species * mostly based on experiments with mammalian orthohantaviruses Viruses assigned to each of the seven genera form genus-specifc monophyletic clades based on phylogenetic analysis of concatenated L protein/RdRP, glycoprotein and N sequences. Viruses from all seven genera share one or more of the following characteristics: (i) enveloped pleomorphic virions; (ii) tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genome without polyadenylated tracts at the 3′-end; (iii) genomic sequence complementarity at the 5′- and 3′-ends; and (iv) capped but not polyadenylated virus mRNAs ( Maes et al., 2004 ). Piscine Hosts Genus Actinovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian (percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) fish. Genus Agnathovirus . Viruses in this genus infect agnathan (myxinid) fish. Genus Percilovirus . Viruses in this genus infect actinopterygian ( gobiid, lophiid ) fish. Mammalian Hosts Genus Loanvirus. Viruses in this genus infect rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly nycterid bats and possibly murid rodents. Genus Mobatvirus. Viruses in this genus infect emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid and possibly molossid, and vespertillionid bats and soricid and talpid eulipotyphla. Genus Orthohantavirus. Viruses assigned to this genus infect soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Genus Thottimvirus. Viruses in this genus infect soricid and possibly talpid eulipotyphla. Reptilian Hosts Genus Reptillovirus . Viruses in this genus infect gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles. Virion Morphology Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Physicochemical and physical properties Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Nucleic acid Hantavirids have tri-segmented, negative-sense RNA genomes (S, M, and L segments). The viral mRNAs are not polyadenylated and contain a 5′-methylated cap and several non-templated nucleotides at the 5′-end that are derived from host cell mRNAs via cap snatching ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Further information is only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Proteins Hantavirids typically express three structural proteins. The most abundant structural protein in a hantavirion is N, which encapsidates the hantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , are produced from GPC and mediate entry of hantavirions ( Schmaljohn et al., 1985 , Spiropoulou 2001 , Vaheri et al., 2013 ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Lipids Not reported but are likely derived from the Golgi apparatus and/or the host cell plasma membrane and therefore likely composed of phospholipids, glycolipids, fatty acids, and sterols. Carbohydrates Only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Genome organization and replication S RNA encodes N and in some viruses NSs ( Jääskeläinen et al., 2007 , Vera-Otarola et al., 2012 ), M RNA encodes GPC, and the L RNA encodes L with its RdRP, helicase, and endonuclease domains ( Jonsson and Schmaljohn 2001 ) (Figure 1 Hantaviridae ). Specifics are only known for members of the genus Orthohantavirus (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Figure 1 Hantaviridae . Genome organization of representative hantaviruses. The 5′- and 3′- ends of all segments are complementary at their termini, likely promoting the formation of panhandle RNP complexes within the virion . GPC , glycoprotein precursor gene; L , large (protein) gene; N , nucleoprotein gene. Biology Hantavirids have been found in actinopterygian (gobiid, lophiid, percid, ogcocephalid, and triacanthodid, and possibly goblid and melanotaeniid) and agnathan (myxinid) fish; in emballonurid, hipposiderid, pteropodid, rhinolophid, verspertillionid, and possibly molossid and nycterid bats; in soricid and talpid eulipotyphla; in muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents; in gekkonid and possibly scincid reptiles; and potentially in coleopteran and plectopteran insects (see genus pages for details). Only orthohantaviruses are known to cause diseases (see Orthohantavirus genus page). Antigenicity Systematic antigenicity studies have only been reported for orthohantaviruses (see Orthohantavirus genus page). species demarcation criteria The availability of at least coding-complete sequences of all three genome segments may be sufficient for hantavirid classification in the absence of a cultured isolate. Demarcation of genera is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Hantaviridae: current classification and future perspectives, Viruses, 11, 9, e0788">Laenen et al., 2019 ). DEmARC analysis gave a frequency distribution of Pairwise Evolutionary Distance (PED) values of which the threshold of 0.1 gave an optimal clustering cost of zero and is used as the hantavirid species demarcation criterium. Genera are demarked by a PED-value threshold of 0.95 and subfamilies are demarcated based on their distinct clustering in a Bayesian maximum clade credibility tree and a PED-value threshold of 3.5. Relationships within the family Phylogenetic relationships across the family have been estimated using Bayesian maximum clade credibility trees generated from complete N, GPC, and L amino-acid sequences; similar topologies are obtained with concatenated N and GPC sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Figure 2 Hantaviridae . Maximum likelihood phylogenetic tree inferred using IQ-TREE. The tree was constructed based on 53 concatenated S and M segment (amino acid) sequences using the LG+R9 model of sequence evolution. Branch lengths represent the estimated number of substitutions per site. Bootstrap support values (>70%) are indicated at nodes, reflecting the degree of confidence in the branching pattern. Relationships with other taxa Hantavirids are closely related to bunyaviral crulivirids, fimovirids, peribunyavirids, phasmavirids, tulasvirids, and tospovirids ( Wolf et al., 2018 , Herath et al., 2020 ). Using the Master Species List Using the Virus Metadata Resource Using the Find the Species tool Using the ICTV Report Webinar Webinar on Virus Taxonomy Webinar on Finding Information GitHub Repository Zenodo Repository Email ICTV Help ‏‏‎ ‎ ICTV Report Book: Hantaviridae Family: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Actantavirinae Genus: Actinovirus Genus: Percilovirus Subfamily: Agantavirinae Genus: Agnathovirus Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Loanvirus Genus: Mobatvirus Genus: Orthohantavirus Genus: Thottimvirus Subfamily: Repantavirinae Genus: Reptillovirus Authors: Hantaviridae Citation: Hantaviridae References: Hantaviridae Resources: Hantaviridae Species List: Hantaviridae Subfamily: Mammantavirinae Genus: Orthohantavirus Distinguishing features Sixty different viruses are classified in the genus Orthohantavius. These viruses typically infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents. Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease in humans ( Schmaljohn and Hjelle 1997 , Jonsson et al., 2010 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 , Vial et al., 2023 ). Virion Morphology Orthohantavirions are pleomorphic in shape, mostly spherical of 80–160 nm in diameter ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ), and surrounded by a membrane envelope that is decorated with glycoprotein (GP) spikes composed of G N and G C subunits (Figure 1 Orthohantavirus ). The virion envelope is 5 nm thick and is decorated with square shaped spikes, consisting of tetrameric G N -G C heterodimers, which protrude 10 nM from the membrane forming a surface lattice of local symmetry interrupted by empty membrane spots ( Hung et al., 1983 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Parvate et al., 2019 , Serris et al., 2020 , Guardado-Calvo and Rey 2021 ). Isolated ribonucleoprotein (RNP) complexes are composed of individual segment genomic RNA encapsidated by nucleoprotein (N) ( Tao et al., 1987 , Huiskonen et al., 2010 , Battisti et al., 2011 , Hepojoki et al., 2012 , Guo et al., 2016 , Arragain et al., 2019 ). Virions assemble and bud from the Golgi complex or cell surface membranes, depending on the virus ( Goldsmith et al., 1995 , Parvate et al., 2019 ). Figure 1 Orthohantavirus. A, B) Electron micrographs of Tula virus particles adapted from ( Huiskonen et al., 2010 ). C) Schematic illustration of an orthohantavirus particle. Shown is a spherical and enveloped (grey) particle with glycoprotein spikes (G N yellow, G C blue) inserted in a bilaminar lipid envelope. The S (small), M (medium), and L (large) RNP (ribonucleoprotein) complexes inside the particle consist of N (nucleoprotein, green) and L (large protein, pink). ViralZone image reproduced courtesy of SwissBioPics. Physicochemical and physical properties Virion buoyant densities in sucrose and CsCl are 1.15–1.18 ( White et al., 1982 ) and 1.20–1.21 g cm −3 , respectively ( Schmaljohn et al., 1983 ). Virions are sensitive to chemical inactivation with, for instance, methanol, paraformaldehyde, acetone/methanol, N -ethylmaleimide or detergents, as well as physical methods such as heat, gamma irradiation or UV irradiation ( Kraus et al., 2005 , Strandin et al., 2011 , Elveborg et al., 2022 ). Nucleic acid Orthohantavirus genomes are linear tri-segmented RNA molecules of negative polarity. The genomes are about 11.1–12.3 kb in length (small [S] segment: 1.2–2.1 kb; medium [M] segment: 3.4–3.8 kb; large [L] segment: 6.5–6.6 kb). Proteins Orthohantaviruses typically express three structural proteins (Table 1 Orthohantavirus ). The most abundant structural protein in an orthohantavirion is N, which encapsidates the orthohantaviral genomic segments. The least abundant protein is L, which mediates viral genome replication and transcription. Two glycoprotein subunits, G N and G C , mediate virion entry. G N and G C and non-structural proteins are encoded as a precursor polyprotein. Table 1 Orthohantavirus . Location and function of orthohantavirus structural proteins. Protein Location, mass, and function Reference Nucleoprotein (N) Structural virion protein (about 48 kD). Oligomerizes and encapsidates orthohantaviral genomic segments and hence component of RNPs. Binds to L and G N ( Mir et al., 2010 , Reuter and Krüger 2018 , Arragain et al., 2019 ) Nonstructural protein (NSs) Non-structural protein encoded by some orhtohantaviruses. Has type I interferon inhibitory activity. May occur as multiple isoforms. ( Vera-Otarola et al., 2020 , Binder et al., 2021 ) Glycoprotein (GP) Structural virion protein consisting of two subunits (G N : about 70-75 kD, G C : about 50-55 kD). Produced via proteolytic cleavage from the genome-encoded precursor GPC. Projects from virion membranes as tetrameric GP spikes composed of G N and G C heterodimers. GP mediates cell- receptor binding; as a class II fusion machine it induces virion-cell membrane fusion and, thereby cell entry. G N binds to N and RNA ( Spiropoulou et al., 2003 , Tischler et al., 2005 , Cifuentes-Muñoz et al., 2014 , Li et al., 2016 , Willensky et al., 2016 , Rissanen et al., 2017 , Zhu et al., 2018 , Bignon et al., 2019 , Sperber et al., 2019 ) Large protein (L) Structural virion protein (246 kD) with RdRP, helicase, and endoribonuclease domains. Component of the RNP inside virions. Binds to N and RNA. Oligomerizes and mediates transcription and replication of viral RNA segments. Mediates cap-snatching for viral mRNA capping. ( Kukkonen et al., 2005 , Cheng et al., 2014 , Rothenberger et al., 2016 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Durieux Trouilleton et al., 2023 ) Genome organization and replication The orthohantavirus genome consists of three negative-sense RNA molecules, termed S (small), M (medium), and L (large) (Figure 2 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 2 Orthohantavirus. Schematic representation of orthohantavirus genome organization. Orthohantavirus genomic segments assume circular forms via non-covalent binding of complementary and highly conserved 3′- and 5′-terminal sequences. Genomic segment reassortment mostly occurs among viruses belonging to the same species but interspecies reassortment likely occurs occasionally ( Klempa 2018 , Petazzi et al., 2021 ). Orthohantavirus infection starts with virion attachment, mediated by G N and G C , to cell-surface attachment factors and entry via the endosomal route ( Shtanko et al., 2014 ) (Figure 3 Orthohantavirus ). Figure 3 Orthohantavirus . Lifecycle of orthohantaviruses. (1) Virion attachment; (2) virion uptake; (3) virion-cell membrane fusion; (4) transcription; (5) translation; (6) replication; (7) virion assembly; and (8) virion egress. After engaging a cellular receptor, protocadherin 1 in the case of American orthohantaviruses, virion-membrane fusion results in early or late endosomal release, depending on the virus, of the virion RNP complex into the cytoplasm in a pH-dependent manner ( Jangra et al., 2018 , Mittler et al., 2019 , Torriani et al., 2019 , Dieterle et al., 2021 ). During primary transcription L generates uncapped antigenomic RNA molecules that are then capped using host cell-derived capped primers (cap snatching). L and S segment-transcribed mRNAs are translated by free ribosomes ( Garcin et al., 1995 , Jeeva et al., 2019 , Meier et al., 2021 ). M segment-transcribed mRNA is translated by membrane-bound ribosomes, with the expressed GPC which is likely co-translationally cleaved by cellular proteases to yield G N and G C . The synthesis of the antigenome by L protein serves as a template for genomic RNA replication. Secondary transcription amplifies the synthesis of mRNAs and genome replication. During morphogenesis, G N and G C accumulate in the Golgi apparatus, modified host membranes are acquired, and virions bud into the Golgi. Biology Genus Orthohantavirus includes 38 species for 60 distinct viruses. These viruses and their unclassified, potential relatives, subclinically, and often chronically, infect specific soricid and talpid eulipotyphla, and muroid and possibly dipodoid rodents ( Jonsson et al., 2010 , Wu et al., 2018 , Chen et al., 2023 , Kuhn and Schmaljohn 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are overall distributed worldwide, but the individual geographic distribution is dependent on host range. At least some orthohantaviruses may not be as restricted to a particular host as originally thought, but may be carried by animals of multiple hosts ( Goodfellow et al., 2021 , Quizon et al., 2022 , Gu et al., 2023 ). Orthohantaviruses are the only hantavirids known to cause disease (all in humans) and all disease-causing viruses are rodent-borne. Human infection may occur after inhalation of aerosolized excreta or secreta of infected rodents or direct rodent contact. The two WHO-recognized orthohantavirus-caused diseases are hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), caused by Asian and European viruses (in particular Dobrava virus [DOBV], Hantaan virus [HTNV], Puumala virus [PUUV] and Seoul virus [SEOV]), and hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a frequently lethal disease caused by viruses from the Americas (in particular Andes virus [ANDV] and Sin Nombre virus [SNV]) ( Vial et al., 2023 ). The hamster model of wild-type ANDV infection is lethal and largely mimics human HPS ( Hooper et al., 2001 ). After SNV infection in nonhuman primates, some animals develop an HPS-like disease, but cell passage of SNV can result in mutations that render the virus non-pathogenic in this model ( Safronetz et al., 2014 ). Many rodent models result in a chronic, asymptomatic infection, and these have been used in early-stage therapeutic studies ( Strandin et al., 2020 ). However, recent advances have been made in development of an HFRS mouse model using HTNV variants ( Wei et al., 2022 ). Orthohantavirus animal models are reviewed in ( Golden et al., 2015 ). Antigenicity There is considerable serum cross-reactivity between the nucleocapsids of hantavirids, but neutralizing antibodies targeting Gn/Gc are more specific. SNV was first identified as a hantavirid based on cross-reactivity of patient sera with other orthohantavirus antigens ( 1993 ). Similarly, rodents that carried SNV were identified in serosurveys using non-SNV orthohantavirus antigens, since SNV had not been isolated at the time ( Childs et al., 1994 ). Species demarcation criteria Demarcation of species is based upon DivErsity pArtitioning by hieRarchical Clustering (DEmARC) analysis) using concatenated deduced S, M, and L segment expression product sequences ( Laenen et al., 2019 ). Phylogenetic relationships across the genus have been estimated using maximum likelihood trees generated from complete N, GPC and L amino-acid sequences, and for N and GPC amino-acid sequences (Figure 2 Hantaviridae ). Hantaviridae ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Hantaviridae (taxid:1980413) VIRION Enveloped, spherical. Diameter from 80 to 120nm. GENOME Segmented Negative-stranded RNA linear genome, L segment is between 6.8 and 12 kb, M segment between 3.2 and 4.9 kb and S segment between 1 and 3 kb. Encodes for four to six proteins. Some hantaviruses also encode a NSs protein on their S segment. GENE EXPRESSION The viral RNA dependent RNA polymerase (L) binds to a promoter on each encapsidated segment, and transcribes the mRNA. These are capped by L protein during synthesis using cap snatching . Transcription is terminated by a strong hairpin sequence at the end of each gene. Puumala virus expressed an additional NSs by leaky scanning in the NS gene. ENZYMES RNA-dependent RNA polymerase L Cap Snatching endonuclease L REPLICATION CYTOPLASMIC Virus attaches to host receptors though Gn-Gc glycoprotein dimer, and is endocytosed into vesicles in the host cell. Fusion of virus membrane with the vesicle membrane; ribonucleocapsid segments are released in the cytoplasm. Transcription , viral mRNAs are capped in the cytoplasm. Replication presumably starts when enough nucleoprotein is present to encapsidate neo-synthetized antigenomes and genomes. The ribonucleocapsids buds at Golgi apparatus, releasing the virion by exocytosis. The hantaviruses (Hantaviridae) ~ ViralZone Skip to main content ViralZone Back to Andes virus resource There are approximately 92 known viruses in the family Hantaviridae, classified into 52 species. Each species is typically adapted to a specific reservoir host, most commonly rodents, but also bats and moles. With the notable exception of Andes virus, hantaviruses are generally not transmitted from person to person. Based on their geographic distribution, evolutionary relationships, and the diseases they cause in humans, hantaviruses can be broadly divided into three major groups: New World hantaviruses (the Americas) These viruses cause Hantavirus pulmonary syndrome (HPS), a severe respiratory disease. Important examples include Sin Nombre virus and Andes virus. Annual incidence are about 100 cases per year (Andes virus) about 25 cases per year (Sin Nombre virus) Old World hantaviruses (Asia) These viruses are responsible for Hantavirus hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS), which is characterized by fever, hemorrhage, and acute kidney injury. Major examples include Hantaan virus and Seoul virus. Annual incidence: more than 10,000 cases worldwide Old World hantaviruses (Europe) European hantaviruses typically cause a milder form of HFRS known as Nephropathia epidemica (NE). The main causative agents are Puumala virus and Dobrava-Belgrade virus. Annual incidence: more than 1,000 cases Together, these viruses represent an important and diverse group of zoonotic pathogens that can cause severe disease following accidental transmission from their natural animal hosts to humans.

papers.title: Andes Virus Exposure and Nosocomial Transmission Events to Healthcare Personnel: A Systematic Review.
papers.abstract: BACKGROUND: Andes virus (ANDV) is a high-consequence infectious disease with substantial mortality. On 2 May 2026, the World Health Organization reported a multinational ANDV outbreak, raising questions regarding the risk of transmission to healthcare personnel (HCP). METHODS: We performed a systematic review per PRISMA guidelines (PROSPERO:CRD420261283806) for studies describing healthcare-associated ANDV exposure or transmission events to HCP. RESULTS: Eight studies reporting on 7 events were included, describing a total of 17 healthcare-associated cases. Overall, 207 individuals were exposed, including 118 HCP, resulting in 8 infections and 4 deaths among HCP. Studies describing HCP infections reported none or inadequate personal protective equipment (PPE) use. CONCLUSIONS: Transmission of ANDV to HCP has been reported in the setting of delayed implementation of transmission-based precautions or breaches in infection control practice. Limitations in published exposure events highlight the need for standardized reporting of exposure events and outcomes as well as infection prevention measures implemented.
papers.journal: Clinical infectious diseases : an official publication of the Infectious Diseases Society of America

analysis.background: ANDV is a high‑consequence pathogen with substantial mortality, and a recent multinational outbreak raised concerns about transmission risk to healthcare personnel.

analysis.future_research: Implement systematic surveillance and standardized reporting of HCP exposures, and evaluate the effectiveness of transmission‑based precautions.

papers.full_text: 이호왕의 유행성출혈열 연구와 한탄바이러스 발견 Ho Wang Lee’s Research of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever and Discovery of Hantaan Virus 6 조회 1 다운로드 0 인용 0 참고문헌 키워드 초록 Abstract This paper argues that Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus as the agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever(EHF) was the result of repeated failures and trials on new objects and new experimental methods. Generally speaking, scientific papers describe the research process as going a straight way leading to the final results. However, researches in the real world are full of trial-and-errors, misunderstandings, and complex interactions among elements in the laboratory. Ho Wang Lee’s research is a good case to show such characteristics of the scientific research.In this paper, Lee’s researches from 1970 to 1980 are examined into three periods. First, from 1970 to 1973, he studied about EHF using wild rats as an experimental object. Wild rats were widely suspected to have the agent of EHF but he failed to get any results. During the second period from 1974 to 1976, he identified an agent of EHF, Korea Antigen, by introducing a new experimental object, the lung of wild rats, and a new method, Fluorescent Antibody Technique. For last 4 years from 1977 to 1980, Lee clarified its physicochemical features. With the results, the Korea Antigen was registered as the agent of EHF, Hantaan Virus in 1980.

Generally speaking, scientific papers describe the research process as going a straight way leading to the final results. However, researches in the real world are full of trial-and-errors, misunderstandings, and complex interactions among elements in the laboratory. Ho Wang Lee’s research is a good case to show such characteristics of the scientific research.In this paper, Lee’s researches from 1970 to 1980 are examined into three periods. First, from 1970 to 1973, he studied about EHF using wild rats as an experimental object. Wild rats were widely suspected to have the agent of EHF but he failed to get any results. During the second period from 1974 to 1976, he identified an agent of EHF, Korea Antigen, by introducing a new experimental object, the lung of wild rats, and a new method, Fluorescent Antibody Technique. analysis.background: The paper examines how Ho Wang Lee discovered the Hantaan virus as the causative agent of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever (EHF), a key step in understanding this severe disease.
analysis.methods: Lee’s work from 1970‑1980 is divided into three periods: (1) 1970‑1973 using whole wild rats (F5); (2) 1974‑1976 introducing lung tissue of wild rats and the Fluorescent Antibody Technique (F7); (3) 1977‑1980 characterizing physicochemical properties of the agent (F8).
analysis.results: Lee identified a novel antigen, termed Korea Antigen, as the EHF agent using the new object and method (F7) and later clarified its physicochemical features, leading to its registration as Hantaan virus in 1980 (F9).
analysis.contribution: The study highlights the trial‑and‑error nature of virological research and documents the historic discovery that established the etiologic link between Hantaan virus and EHF, informing future surveillance and clinical work.
analysis.limitations: The article provides only an abstract and partial text, lacking detailed experimental data, quantitative results, or broader contextual information.

analysis.summary_en: Background: The paper reviews Ho Wang Lee’s discovery of Hantaan virus as the cause of Epidemic Hemorrhagic Fever, a critical step for disease understanding. Methods: Lee’s research (1970‑1980) progressed from using whole wild rats, to lung tissue with Fluorescent Antibody Technique, and finally physicochemical characterization. Results: He identified Korea Antigen as the EHF agent and, after further study, registered it as Hantaan virus in 1980. Contribution: The work illustrates the iterative nature of virology and records a landmark finding that underpins surveillance and clinical response to EHF. Limitations: Only an abstract and partial text are available, so detailed data and broader analysis are not reported.

papers.title: Hantavirus at the Climate–Rodent–Human Interface: Integrating Immunopathogenesis, Ecological Drivers, and Health Inequities in the Americas
papers.abstract: New World orthohantaviruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HCPS) within heterogeneous ecological and healthcare settings across the Americas. This selective critical narrative review integrates rodent reservoir ecology, environmental and occupational exposure, immunopathogenesis, and structural determinants of detection and care. Evidence is unevenly distributed, with detailed investigations concentrated in the United States, Panama, Chile, Argentina, and Brazil. Climate variability, land-use change, housing, and occupational conditions are associated with context-dependent exposure opportunities, not a uniform continental risk gradient. Protocadherin-1-dependent entry is experimentally supported for Andes virus (ANDV) and Sin Nombre virus (SNV). Endothelial barrier dysfunction is central to severe HCPS, whereas associations involving inflammatory cytokines, natural killer-cell phenotypes, and antibody Fc-effector functions have not established causation or validated prognostic utility. Geographic remoteness, diagnostic turnaround, and critical-care access are plausible modifiers of observed outcomes, although direct comparative estimates of their contributions to mortality disparities are limited. Findings in distinct Indigenous communities reflect heterogeneous ecological and structural contexts and do not demonstrate intrinsic biological susceptibility. We propose a testable mechanism-to-population One Health framework linking reservoir circulation, human exposure, early infection, vascular injury, case ascertainment, and care pathways. Proposed surveillance indicators and interventions require prospective, locally calibrated evaluation with community engagement.

analysis.summary_en: Background: New World orthohantaviruses cause HCPS across diverse ecological and healthcare contexts in the Americas. Future research: Prospective, locally calibrated surveillance and community‑engaged interventions are required to evaluate the One Health mechanism‑to‑population framework.

analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述整合了啮齿动物宿主生态、环境与职业暴露、免疫发病机制以及检测和护理的结构性决定因素。
analysis_zh.current_state: 内皮屏障功能障碍是重症 HCPS 的核心,实验支持 安第斯病毒 与 Sin Nombre 病毒通过 protocadherin‐1 依赖性进入,但许多免疫相关指标缺乏因果验证。
analysis_zh.gaps: 气候变异、土地利用变化、住房和职业条件导致情境依赖的暴露,关于偏远程度、诊断延迟和重症监护获取如何影响死亡率差异的定量数据有限。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要前瞻性、当地校准的监测指标和干预措施,并与社区共同设计,以检验所提出的 One Health 机制‐到‐人群框架。

papers.title: Framing Krisis Hantavirus dalam Komunikasi Pemasaran Pariwisata
papers.abstract: This study examines how English-language online media in Indonesia frame the hantavirus crisis involving MV Hondius and how such framing is relevant to tourism marketing communication during a transnational health crisis. Using qualitative content analysis and framing analysis, the study analyzes 16 unique and relevant news articles archived from Jakarta Globe and The Jakarta Post between 4 and 31 May 2026 with the keywords “MV Hondius”, “hantavirus”, and “Andes virus”. The corpus was selected from 27 initial publications through purposive sampling, relevance screening, and deduplication. The articles were coded according to publication phase, dominant frame, actor visibility, risk emphasis, and marketing communication implications. The findings show that the news did not merely report a medical event but constructed a crisis narrative that moved from outbreak escalation to cross-border control and reputational normalization. The dominant frame was cross-national governance, followed by reputational recovery, tourism mobility, and health threat. The study argues that tourism crisis messages should combine health accuracy, mobility transparency, destination reassurance, and evidence-based reputation recovery within an eco-systemic crisis communication perspective.

papers.full_text: MUKASI: Jurnal Ilmu Komunikasi https://journal.yp3a.org/index.php/MUKASI e-ISSN 2828-3449 | p-ISSN 2828-3589 Vol. 5 No. 4 (November 2026) 2016-2030 DOI: 10.54259/mukasi.v5i4.8206 Submitted: 14-06-2026 | Accepted: 19-09-2026 | Published: 15-11-2026 2016 Framing Krisis Hantavirus dalam Komunikasi Pemasaran Pariwisata Satria Hidayat Suryo Pramono1, Dwi Prasetyo2* 1,2Program Studi Ilmu Komunikasi, Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Surabaya, Indonesia Email: 1satria.hidayat2004@gmail.com, 2*dwiprasetyo@unesa.ac.id Abstract This study examines how English-language online media in Indonesia frame the hantavirus crisis involving MV Hondius and how such framing is relevant to tourism marketing communication during a transnational health crisis. Using qualitative content analysis and framing analysis, the study analyzes 16 unique and relevant news articles archived from Jakarta Globe and The Jakarta Post between 4 and 31 May 2026 with the keywords “MV Hondius”, “hantavirus”, and “Andes virus”. The corpus was selected from 27 initial publications through purposive sampling, relevance screening, and deduplication. The articles were coded according to publication phase, dominant frame, actor visibility, risk emphasis, and marketing communication implications. The findings show that the news did not merely report a medical event but constructed a crisis narrative that moved from outbreak escalation to cross-border control and reputational normalization. The dominant frame was cross-national governance, followed by reputational recovery, tourism mobility, and health threat. The study argues that tourism crisis messages should combine health accuracy, mobility transparency, destination reassurance, and evidence-based reputation recovery within an eco-systemic crisis communication perspective. Keywords: Crisis Communication, Destination Reputation, Framing Analysis, Marketing Communication, Tourism Safety Campaign Abstrak Penelitian ini menganalisis bagaimana media daring berbahasa Inggris di Indonesia membingkai krisis hantavirus pada kapal MV Hondius serta relevansinya bagi komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata dalam situasi krisis kesehatan lintas negara. Dengan menggunakan analisis isi kualitatif dan analisis framing, penelitian ini mengkaji 16 berita unik dan relevan dari Jakarta Globe dan The Jakarta Post pada periode 4–31 Mei 2026 dengan kata kunci “MV Hondius”, “hantavirus”, dan “Andes virus”. Korpus dipilih dari 27 publikasi awal melalui purposive sampling, penyaringan relevansi, dan deduplikasi. Artikel dianalisis berdasarkan fase publikasi, frame dominan, visibilitas aktor, penekanan risiko, dan implikasi komunikasi pemasaran. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa pemberitaan tidak hanya melaporkan peristiwa medis, tetapi juga membangun narasi krisis yang bergerak dari eskalasi wabah, kontrol lintas negara, hingga normalisasi reputasi. Frame dominan adalah tata kelola lintas negara, diikuti pemulihan reputasi, mobilitas pariwisata, dan ancaman kesehatan. Temuan ini menegaskan perlunya pesan krisis pariwisata yang mengintegrasikan akurasi kesehatan, transparansi mobilitas, penenangan destinasi, dan pemulihan reputasi berbasis bukti. Satria Hidayat Suryo Pramono1, Dwi Prasetyo2 MUKASI (Jurnal Ilmu Komunikasi) Vol. 5 No. 4 (2026) 2016 – 2030 Lisensi: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) 2017 Kata Kunci: Komunikasi Krisis, Reputasi Destinasi, Analisis Framing, Komunikasi Pemasaran, Kampanye Keselamatan Pariwisata PENDAHULUAN Pariwisata modern bergantung pada mobilitas manusia, kepercayaan publik, dan citra destinasi yang dibangun melalui berbagai kanal komunikasi. Ketika sebuah krisis kesehatan muncul pada ruang mobilitas wisata, terutama kapal pesiar internasional, persoalannya tidak berhenti pada dimensi medis. Krisis tersebut segera berubah menjadi persoalan komunikasi karena khalayak, calon wisatawan, institusi kesehatan, otoritas perbatasan, operator perjalanan, dan media massa sama-sama berusaha mendefinisikan tingkat bahaya, pihak yang bertanggung jawab, serta kemungkinan pemulihan. Dalam konteks inilah komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata tidak dapat dipahami hanya sebagai promosi, melainkan sebagai proses strategis untuk mempertahankan kepercayaan, mengelola persepsi risiko, dan menjaga reputasi destinasi di tengah ketidakpastian dalam ekosistem komunikasi krisis yang melibatkan banyak actor (Hu & Li, 2022;Wu & Li, 2022) Wabah hantavirus yang diberitakan terkait MV Hondius pada Mei 2026 memperlihatkan kompleksitas tersebut. Berita yang terkumpul menunjukkan bahwa satu peristiwa kesehatan pada kapal pesiar dapat bergerak cepat dari pemberitaan mengenai penyakit, kematian, dan dugaan penularan, menuju isu evakuasi, karantina, skrining bandara, perjalanan lintas negara, hingga pembersihan kapal dan penilaian risiko rendah. Pergerakan narasi ini penting bagi kajian komunikasi pemasaran karena reputasi pariwisata sering kali dibentuk bukan hanya oleh apa yang dilakukan destinasi atau operator wisata, tetapi juga oleh bagaimana media menyeleksi fakta, menghubungkan aktor, serta menonjolkan konsekuensi tertentu. Literatur komunikasi krisis kesehatan menunjukkan bahwa krisis mengancam kepercayaan publik ketika informasi risiko tidak disampaikan secara jelas, konsisten, dan dapat diverifikasi. Dalam pariwisata, dampaknya lebih luas karena wisatawan mengambil keputusan berdasarkan persepsi keamanan, kredibilitas institusi, dan kemampuan aktor perjalanan untuk mengendalikan risiko. Pandemi COVID-19 memperlihatkan bahwa pariwisata sangat rentan terhadap gangguan kesehatan global serta membutuhkan strategi pemulihan yang tidak hanya operasional, tetapi juga komunikatif. Oleh karena itu, peristiwa hantavirus pada kapal pesiar dapat dibaca sebagai kasus mikro yang mempertemukan komunikasi kesehatan, komunikasi krisis, framing media, dan komunikasi pemasaran destinasi dalam satu jaringan komunikasi krisis yang bersifat lintas institusi dan lintas negara. Masalah utama dalam banyak krisis pariwisata adalah jarak antara fakta kesehatan dan persepsi publik. Informasi mengenai jumlah kasus, lokasi kapal, negara asal penumpang, hasil tes, atau status disinfeksi dapat ditafsirkan secara berbeda tergantung cara media menyusunnya. Studi framing kesehatan kontemporer menunjukkan bahwa media dapat menonjolkan ancaman, aktor, penyebab, dan solusi tertentu sehingga khalayak diarahkan untuk memahami krisis melalui skema interpretatif tertentu. Dengan demikian, analisis terhadap pemberitaan hantavirus bukan hanya analisis isi berita, melainkan analisis atas konstruksi makna yang dapat mempengaruhi cara publik memandang keamanan perjalanan dan reputasi sektor pariwisata. Kajian mengenai komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata selama krisis umumnya menyoroti pemulihan destinasi, promosi pascakrisis, atau manajemen reputasi organisasi. Namun, masih terdapat celah riset pada bagaimana pemberitaan media berbahasa Inggris di Indonesia membingkai krisis kesehatan transnasional yang melibatkan kapal pesiar, negara-negara transit, dan otoritas kesehatan internasional, serta bagaimana Satria Hidayat Suryo Pramono1, Dwi Prasetyo2 MUKASI (Jurnal Ilmu Komunikasi) Vol. 5 No. 4 (2026) 2016 – 2030 Lisensi: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) 2018 pembingkaian tersebut dapat dibaca sebagai bahan strategis bagi komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata. Celah ini penting karena media berbahasa Inggris di Indonesia tidak hanya berfungsi sebagai kanal pemberitaan, tetapi juga sebagai gatekeeper informasi bagi pelancong internasional, ekspatriat, investor asing, operator perjalanan, dan pengambil kebijakan yang membutuhkan rujukan cepat mengenai keamanan mobilitas wisata. Dalam perspektif eco-systemic crisis communication, media semacam ini menempati posisi strategis karena menghubungkan informasi dari otoritas kesehatan, operator kapal, negara transit, bandara, destinasi, dan pasar wisata global ke dalam satu ekosistem makna krisis. Dengan demikian, Jakarta Globe dan The Jakarta Post relevan dikaji karena keduanya dapat memediasi bagaimana krisis kapal pesiar transnasional dibaca oleh audiens internasional yang berkepentingan terhadap reputasi pariwisata Indonesia dan kawasan sekitarnya. Penelitian ini bertujuan menganalisis frame dominan dalam pemberitaan Jakarta Globe dan The Jakarta Post tentang krisis hantavirus MV Hondius serta merumuskan implikasinya bagi komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata. Penelitian ini berargumen bahwa pemberitaan krisis kesehatan pariwisata membentuk dua fungsi komunikasi yang tampak berlawanan namun saling berkaitan, yaitu amplifikasi risiko dan pemulihan reputasi. Pada satu sisi, media menonjolkan bahaya, jumlah kasus, kematian, dan ketidakpastian epidemiologis. Pada sisi lain, media juga menghadirkan aktor institusional, prosedur pengendalian, hasil tes negatif, disinfeksi, dan penilaian risiko rendah sebagai dasar pembentukan kembali kepercayaan (Hu & Li, 2022;Wu & Li, 2022). Kontribusi penelitian ini bersifat konseptual dan praktis. Secara konseptual, penelitian ini menghubungkan framing media dengan komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata dalam konteks krisis kesehatan lintas negara melalui perspektif eco-systemic crisis communication yang menempatkan media, otoritas kesehatan, operator wisata, destinasi, dan khalayak internasional sebagai bagian dari ekosistem komunikasi yang saling memengaruhi. Secara praktis, hasil penelitian menawarkan pemahaman tentang jenis pesan yang perlu diprioritaskan oleh destinasi, operator kapal pesiar, otoritas bandara, dan institusi kesehatan ketika pemberitaan media mulai membentuk persepsi publik. Dengan membaca media sebagai arena pembentukan reputasi, komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata dapat bergerak dari logika promosi menuju logika trust-building yang berbasis bukti, koordinasi, dan transparansi Dalam situasi krisis, media tidak hanya menjadi saluran informasi, tetapi juga menjadi arena kompetisi interpretasi. Aktor institusional dapat mengeluarkan rilis resmi, operator perjalanan dapat menyampaikan pernyataan keselamatan, dan otoritas kesehatan dapat memberi penilaian risiko. Namun, khalayak sering kali memahami keseluruhan situasi melalui berita yang merangkum berbagai pernyataan tersebut. Karena itu, pemberitaan berfungsi sebagai jembatan antara data teknis dan persepsi publik. Apabila jembatan ini menekankan konflik atau ketidakpastian, reputasi pariwisata dapat tertekan. Apabila jembatan ini menekankan koordinasi dan bukti pengendalian, reputasi memiliki peluang untuk dipulihkan karena media membantu mengubah informasi teknis menjadi narasi publik yang dapat dipahami oleh pasar wisata (Garaus & Hudakova, 2022). Konteks kapal pesiar juga menjadikan kasus ini bernilai analitis. Kapal pesiar merupakan produk wisata yang menggabungkan akomodasi, transportasi, hiburan, dan mobilitas lintas negara dalam satu ruang tertutup. Model wisata ini menawarkan pengalaman yang terintegrasi, tetapi pada saat krisis kesehatan ia dapat dipersepsikan sebagai ruang yang rentan karena penumpang dan kru berada dalam lingkungan bersama dalam jangka waktu tertentu. Oleh sebab itu, framing media terhadap kapal pesiar memiliki implikasi langsung terhadap persepsi keamanan produk wisata dan bukan hanya terhadap destinasi tertentu. Satria Hidayat Suryo Pramono1, Dwi Prasetyo2 MUKASI (Jurnal Ilmu Komunikasi) Vol. 5 No. 4 (2026) 2016 – 2030 Lisensi: Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) 2019 Selain itu, penggunaan media berbahasa Inggris di Indonesia memberi konteks komunikasi internasional yang khas. Pemberitaan dalam bahasa Inggris memungkinkan isu lokal atau regional dibaca oleh khalayak global, termasuk pelaku industri pariwisata internasional. Dengan demikian, artikel ini tidak hanya membaca bagaimana media nasional membingkai isu, tetapi juga bagaimana sebuah isu kesehatan global diterjemahkan ke dalam ruang komunikasi Indonesia yang terhubung dengan pasar global. Dari sudut pandang marketing communication, hal ini menunjukkan bahwa reputasi pariwisata tidak selalu dibangun melalui kampanye resmi, tetapi juga melalui pemberitaan yang dapat diakses lintas negara dan berfungsi sebagai rujukan reputasional bagi pasar wisata internasional (Liu et al., 2023;Mele et al., 2023). TINJAUAN PUSTAKA Framing merupakan salah satu konsep utama dalam kajian komunikasi massa karena menjelaskan bagaimana media mengorganisasi realitas sosial melalui seleksi isu, penonjolan aktor, pilihan istilah, dan struktur naratif. Dalam pemberitaan krisis kesehatan, framing menjadi penting karena media dapat membuat suatu peristiwa dibaca sebagai ancaman medis, masalah mobilitas, kegagalan tata kelola, atau situasi yang sedang dikendalikan. Kajian terhadap framing COVID-19 menunjukkan bahwa isu kesehatan dapat dibangun melalui metafora, kategori ancaman, bahasa perang, dan penekanan pada tindakan kolektif. Kerangka ini relevan untuk membaca pemberitaan MV Hondius karena setiap berita tidak hanya menyajikan fakta, tetapi juga mengatur urutan makna tentang bahaya, tanggung jawab, dan pemulihan dalam ruang komunikasi yang dibaca oleh publik lintas negara. Dalam komunikasi strategis dan public relations, framing dapat dipahami sebagai proses pembentukan konteks yang memengaruhi bagaimana organisasi, otoritas publik, dan khalayak memahami krisis. Krisis pariwisata yang melibatkan penyakit menular dapat muncul dalam beberapa bingkai sekaligus: ancaman kesehatan, mobilitas wisata, tanggung jawab operator, respons pemerintah, dan pemulihan reputasi. Studi komunikasi kesehatan pada masa pandemi menegaskan bahwa bingkai media memengaruhi orientasi publik terhadap risiko, sumber otoritatif, dan tindakan yang dianggap tepat. Oleh sebab itu, analisis framing dalam artikel ini diarahkan untuk memahami bagaimana pemberitaan menghubungkan risiko kesehatan dengan citra pariwisata, terutama ketika media berfungsi sebagai penghubung antara informasi teknis kesehatan dan persepsi pasar wisata internasional (Garaus & Hudakova, 2022). Komunikasi krisis memberikan kerangka untuk memahami hubungan antara ancaman, reputasi, dan respons publik. Dalam kasus pariwisata, reputasi tidak hanya melekat pada satu organisasi, tetapi dapat menyebar pada destinasi, pelabuhan, negara transit, jenis perjalanan, bahkan kategori produk wisata seperti kapal pesiar. Literatur mutakhir tentang komunikasi risiko kesehatan menekankan bahwa kredibilitas respons bergantung pada kecepatan informasi, konsistensi sumber, pengakuan terhadap ketidakpastian, serta kemampuan menyajikan tindakan korektif yang dapat diperiksa. Karena itu, komunikasi krisis pariwisata harus memperhatikan efek asosiasi yang dapat memperluas kerusakan reputasi dari satu titik peristiwa ke ekosistem perjalanan yang lebih luas serta membaca krisis sebagai proses komunikasi eco-systemic, yaitu proses yang melibatkan relasi antara otoritas kesehatan, operator perjalanan, destinasi, media, wisatawan, dan pasar internasional (Hu & Li, 2022;Wu & Li, 2022). Prinsip komunikasi risiko pada situasi darurat menekankan kebutuhan informasi yang cepat, akurat, empatik, dan dapat dipercaya. Dalam pemberitaan kesehatan lintas negara, prinsip ini menjadi relevan karena informasi yang terlambat, tidak konsisten, atau terlalu menenangkan tanpa bukti dapat menimbulkan resistensi. Studi komunikasi kesehatan selama COVID-19 menunjukkan bahwa kejelasan otoritas, koordinasi pesan, dan pengakuan atas ketidakpastian merupakan prasyarat agar publik dapat menilai risiko secara proporsional. Hal ini sejalan dengan kebutuhan komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata selama krisis, yakni menenangkan tanpa menutupi risiko, serta menampilkan bukti pengendalian yang dapat diverifikasi oleh publik dan media (Mele et al., 2023). Komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata pada situasi krisis memiliki karakter yang berbeda dari komunikasi pemasaran rutin. Dalam situasi normal, pesan pemasaran banyak menonjolkan daya tarik destinasi, pengalaman, diferensiasi, dan nilai emosional. Dalam situasi krisis, pesan harus membangun kembali syarat dasar konsumsi wisata, yaitu rasa aman dan percaya. Literatur pariwisata pascapandemi menunjukkan bahwa pemulihan sektor wisata bergantung pada kemampuan aktor destinasi untuk mengelola risiko, menjelaskan protokol, dan menciptakan kembali keyakinan wisatawan terhadap mobilitas. Dengan demikian, pesan pemasaran pada masa krisis perlu bergeser dari attraction-based message menuju safety-based message, yaitu pesan yang menonjolkan kesiapan, prosedur, koordinasi otoritas, dan bukti keselamatan. Krisis kesehatan juga memperlihatkan bahwa reputasi destinasi dipengaruhi oleh relasi antara komunikasi institusional dan pemberitaan media. Pariwisata global terbukti sangat rentan terhadap krisis kesehatan karena mobilitas manusia, batas negara, kepercayaan pasar, dan infrastruktur perjalanan saling terhubung. full_text_sections.full_text: MUKASI: Jurnal Ilmu Komunikasi https://journal.yp3a.org/index.php/MUKASI e-ISSN 2828-3449 | p-ISSN 2828-3589 Vol. 5 No. 4 (November 2026) 2016-2030 DOI: 10.54259/mukasi.v5i4.8206 Submitted: 14-06-2026 | Accepted: 19-09-2026 | Published: 15-11-2026 2016 Framing Krisis Hantavirus dalam Komunikasi Pemasaran Pariwisata Satria Hidayat Suryo Pramono1, Dwi Prasetyo2* 1,2Program Studi Ilmu Komunikasi, Universitas Negeri Surabaya, Surabaya, Indonesia Email: 1satria.hidayat2004@gmail.com, 2*dwiprasetyo@unesa.ac.id Abstract This study examines how English-language online media in Indonesia frame the hantavirus crisis involving MV Hondius and how such framing is relevant to tourism marketing communication during a transnational health crisis. Using qualitative content analysis and framing analysis, the study analyzes 16 unique and relevant news articles archived from Jakarta Globe and The Jakarta Post between 4 and 31 May 2026 with the keywords “MV Hondius”, “hantavirus”, and “Andes virus”. The corpus was selected from 27 initial publications through purposive sampling, relevance screening, and deduplication. The articles were coded according to publication phase, dominant frame, actor visibility, risk emphasis, and marketing communication implications. The findings show that the news did not merely report a medical event but constructed a crisis narrative that moved from outbreak escalation to cross-border control and reputational normalization. The dominant frame was cross-national governance, followed by reputational recovery, tourism mobility, and health threat. The study argues that tourism crisis messages should combine health accuracy, mobility transparency, destination reassurance, and evidence-based reputation recovery within an eco-systemic crisis communication perspective. Keywords: Crisis Communication, Destination Reputation, Framing Analysis, Marketing Communication, Tourism Safety Campaign Abstrak Penelitian ini menganalisis bagaimana media daring berbahasa Inggris di Indonesia membingkai krisis hantavirus pada kapal MV Hondius serta relevansinya bagi komunikasi pemasaran pariwisata dalam situasi krisis kesehatan lintas negara. Dengan menggunakan analisis isi kualitatif dan analisis framing, penelitian ini mengkaji 16 berita unik dan relevan dari Jakarta Globe dan The Jakarta Post pada periode 4–31 Mei 2026 dengan kata kunci “MV Hondius”, “hantavirus”, dan “Andes virus”. Korpus dipilih dari 27 publikasi awal melalui purposive sampling, penyaringan relevansi, dan deduplikasi. Artikel dianalisis berdasarkan fase publikasi, frame dominan, visibilitas aktor, penekanan risiko, dan implikasi komunikasi pemasaran. Hasil penelitian menunjukkan bahwa pemberitaan tidak hanya melaporkan peristiwa medis, tetapi juga membangun narasi krisis yang bergerak dari eskalasi wabah, kontrol lintas negara, hingga normalisasi reputasi. Frame dominan adalah tata kelola lintas negara, diikuti pemulihan reputasi, mobilitas pariwisata, dan ancaman kesehatan. Temuan ini menegaskan perlunya pesan krisis pariwisata yang mengintegrasikan akurasi kesehatan, transparansi mobilitas, penenangan destinasi, dan pemulihan reputasi berbasis bukti. papers.title_zh: 在旅游营销传播中的危机框架 汉坦病毒

analysis_zh.background: 本文研究印尼的英文在线媒体如何对邮轮 MV Hondius 上的 汉坦病毒 疫情进行框架化,以及在跨国健康危机期间,此类框架为何对旅游营销传播具有重要意义。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者对2026年5月4日至31日发布的来自 Jakarta Globe 和 The Jakarta Post 的16篇独立新闻报道进行定性内容与框架分析,这些报道从最初的27篇文献中通过目的抽样、相关性筛选和去重后选出。
analysis_zh.results: 分析显示,新闻叙事从疫情升级演变至跨境管控和声誉正常化,主导框架为跨国治理,其次是声誉恢复、旅游流动性以及健康威胁。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究建议,旅游危机信息应在生态系统危机传播视角下,融合健康准确性、流动性透明度、目的地安抚以及基于证据的声誉恢复。
analysis_zh.limitations: 在提供的证据中未报告局限性;缺乏编码员可靠性、更广泛媒体抽样或定量验证等细节。

papers.title: Learning from COVID-19 to strengthen hantavirus preparedness and public health response
papers.abstract: Years after the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, the world continues to face significant health, social, and economic challenges, while emerging and re-emerging infectious diseases remain a growing global public health concern. This trend highlights the importance of interconnected health systems and reveals both the strengths and weaknesses of global public health preparedness and response. In this context, we present a comparative analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent Andes virus outbreak, focusing on their epidemiological and virological characteristics, and discussing the effectiveness of the COVID-19 public health responses. We also explore key lessons that can be applied to future zoonotic threats in the context of rapidly changing ecosystems. The results reveal that COVID-19 and hantavirus infections share several molecular and clinical features but differ in their transmission patterns. COVID-19 spreads efficiently between humans and caused a global pandemic, whereas Hantavirus infections are mainly transmitted from rodents to humans and remain geographically localized despite a higher case fatality rate. While vaccines are available for COVID-19, none exist for Hantavirus disease. The study also highlights the value of artificial intelligence, epidemic intelligence, and the One Health approach for improving outbreak prediction, detection, and surveillance.

This trend highlights the importance of interconnected health systems and reveals both the strengths and weaknesses of global public health preparedness and response. In this context, we present a comparative analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent Andes virus outbreak, focusing on their epidemiological and virological characteristics, and discussing the effectiveness of the COVID-19 public health responses. We also explore key lessons that can be applied to future zoonotic threats in the context of rapidly changing ecosystems. The results reveal that COVID-19 and hantavirus infections share several molecular and clinical features but differ in their transmission patterns. COVID-19 spreads efficiently between humans and caused a global pandemic, whereas Hantavirus infections are mainly transmitted from rodents to humans and remain geographically localized despite a higher case fatality rate. While vaccines are available for COVID-19, none exist for Hantavirus disease. The study also highlights the value of artificial intelligence, epidemic intelligence, and the One Health approach for improving outbreak prediction, detection, and surveillance. Keywords Artificial intelligence, COVID-19, Hantavirus, One health, Public health, Zoonotic disease ​1 Introduction Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic diseases caused by both novel and known patho­ gens are increasingly recognized as a major global public health concern [1]. Zoonoses are infectious diseases that can be transmitted between animals and humans through direct or indirect contact. They are caused by a broad range of pathogens, including bac­ teria, viruses, parasites, fungi, rickettsia, chlamydia, mycoplasma, and other infectious agents. Some zoonotic pathogens have multiple animal reservoir hosts that contribute to their maintenance and transmission by supporting pathogen persistence, amplification, Page 2 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 and spillover to humans. Zoonotic infections are estimated to cause approximately 2.7 million deaths each year, underscoring their substantial impact on global health [2, 3]. Environmental modifications, including deforestation, habitat fragmentation, agri­ cultural expansion, irrigation, urbanization, and climate change disrupt ecosystems and increase contact between humans and wildlife, and have given birth to zoonotic diseases, such as malaria and Lyme disease, thereby facilitating pathogen spillover. Changes in the abundance and distribution of animal hosts can strongly influence the occurrence and transmission of zoonotic diseases in humans. For example, El Niño events in 1991–1992 and 1997–1998 in the southwestern United States (U.S) increased precipitation and veg­ etation growth, providing more food for rodents and resulting in a substantial increase in rodent populations. This ecological cascade favored hantavirus transmission among rodents and subsequently contributed to an increase in human hantavirus cases [3]. At the same time, population growth and the increasing demand for food have increased human exposure to food-borne zoonotic pathogens. Although wildlife contributes less to global food consumption than domestic livestock, the trade and consumption of wild­ life can increase opportunities for pathogens to cross species barriers. For instance, in Europe, changes in vegetation, food availability, water resources, climate, and land use can increase rodent populations and human exposure [4]. In Argentina, climate change and habitat fragmentation have been linked to recent increases in cases by favoring rodent reservoirs [5], either directly (via winter survival) or indirectly (through food lim­ itation). Studies have also shown a positive association between bank vole density and PUUV prevalence [6]. Similarly, in Brazil and the western U.S, Hantavirus occurrence has been associated with socioeconomic factors, environmental conditions, and rodent diversity [7]. Due to environment disruption, several zoonotic diseases have demon­ strated their potential to cause severe outbreaks and widespread public health impacts, including hantavirus infections, Mpox, Ebola virus disease, and Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) [2, 3]. COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, provides a major example of a zoonotic disease with global health consequences. SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, where early investigations suggested an epidemiological association between the initial cases and seafood and live-animal markets. Bats are considered a likely natural reservoir of related coronaviruses, while the potential role of other animals, including pangolins, as intermediate hosts remains uncertain and continues to be investigated [8, 9]. The COVID-19 pandemic placed zoonotic diseases at the forefront of global atten­ tion, demonstrating how disruptions at the human–animal–environment interface can have profound health, social, and economic consequences [3]. It underscored the impor­ tance of understanding these interconnected systems and exposed both the strengths and limitations of global public health preparedness and response capacities [10]. Recently, the world has experienced a new hantavirus outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV), associated with the cruise ship MV Hondius, which departed from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1, 2026, and followed a South Atlantic itinerary before arriving in Cabo Verde [11, 12]. The outbreak was particularly significant not because it indicated pandemic-level transmissibility, but because it combined a severe zoonotic infection with delayed and nonspecific early symptoms, highly mobile international contacts, limited medical capacity aboard the ship, complex multijurisdictional oversight, and increased public Page 3 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 sensitivity to infectious disease outbreaks following the COVID-19 pandemic [13]. This raises an important question: how effective was the public health response to COVID- 19, and what lessons can be applied to the 2026 ANDV outbreak as a contemporary case study in a rapidly changing ecosystem? To address this question, this review adopts a comparative analysis by examining the epidemiological, virological, ecological, and public health dimensions of both diseases from an integrated multidisciplinary and environmental perspective. The literature search was initiated on 10 May 2026 and was continuously updated throughout the revision process to incorporate newly published and relevant evidence. Searches were conducted across major scientific databases, including PubMed and Google Scholar, supplemented by information from authoritative public health agencies, including the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), using combinations of keywords related to “COVID-19”, “hanta­ virus”, “immunopathogenesis”, “diagnosis,” “surveillance” and “One Health”, along with additional search terms tailored to each specific subtopic. Ecological analyses and diag­ nostic evaluation studies were also considered. To minimize selection bias, study screen­ ing and eligibility assessment were performed independently by all the authors, with disagreements resolved through discussion. A predefined quality assessment was also applied to evaluate the methodological robustness and relevance of the included stud­ ies. Reference lists of relevant articles were also screened to identify additional studies. Sources were eligible for inclusion if they addressed one or more of these aspects and provided relevant evidence for understanding the similarities and differences between COVID-19 and hantavirus infections, as well as lessons for strengthening preparedness and public health responses to emerging zoonotic diseases. 2 Epidemiology In 2019, the new Coronavirus (CoV), SARS-CoV-2, has emerged, and rapidly spread globally. The WHO declared COVID-19 a pandemic on 11 March 2020 [8, 9]. The global COVID-19 numbers reported since the beginning of the pandemic until April 13, 2024 show a total of 704,753,890 cases, with 7,010,681 deaths and 675,619,811 recovered. After this date, the majority of countries have stopped reporting the COVID-19 statis­ tics. The peak reached 3,848,199 cases/daily on January 20, 2022 [14]. In Europe, the excess mortality rates ranged between 14.9% and 54.3% in 2020, with most of the deaths occurred in the eastern part of Europe. In May 2023, the excess mortality was reported to be 3.7% [15]. The mortality rate in America was 1% whereas the case fatality rates (CFRs) in Africa region were the lowest, ranging from 1.214% to 2.548% in 2022, and from 1.18% to 2.516% in 2024, as American and African countries were the last regions in the world to be affected by COVID-19. In Asia, the CFR ranged from 0.359% to 1.467% in 2022 and from 0.346% to 2.516% in 2024 [16–18]. SARS-CoV-2 was not the first CoV identified. CoVs are widespread viruses that infect both humans and animals, including birds and mammals, and are responsible for a substantial proportion of com­ mon cold cases. Before the emergence of SARS-CoV-2, six human coronaviruses were known: four typically caused mild respiratory illnesses, whereas two—SARS-CoV and MERS-CoV—were associated with severe and sometimes fatal disease [19]. Regarding the recent ANDV outbreak, a cluster of passengers presenting with severe respiratory illness aboard the vessel was reported to the WHO on 2 May 2026. The ship Page 4 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 was carrying 147 passengers and crew members. By 4 May 2026, seven hantavirus- related cases had been identified, including two laboratory-confirmed infections and five suspected cases. Among these cases, three deaths were reported, one patient was in critical condition, and three individuals presented with mild symptoms [11]. As of 2 July, a total of 13 cases had been reported, including three deaths, corresponding to a CFR of 23%. Twelve cases were laboratory-confirmed for ANDV infection, while one was classified as a probable case [20]. The reported cases included four Dutch, three British, two Spanish, one German, one Swiss, one French, and one Canadian national. Similar to CoVs, hantaviruses are not newly emerging pathogens; rather, they have long been recognized as important zoonotic viruses with established reservoirs and diverse trans­ mission patterns [21]. The infection appears to have been described in Chinese literature nearly 900 years ago, but gained global attention during the Korean War (1950–1953) [22, 23], when more than 3,000 United Nations soldiers developed hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS). Major outbreaks were also reported during World War II and the Balkan War, particularly among soldiers in Europe and Asia. The causative agent, Hantaan virus (HTNV), was identified in the early 1980s present in the lungs of its natural reservoir, the striped field mouse (Apodemus agrarius). Overall, an estimated 10,000 to more than 100,000 Hantavirus infections occur worldwide each year, with the highest burden reported in Asia and Europe [24]. HFRS remains responsible for thou­ sands of annual cases, particularly in Asia and Europe, whereas hantavirus cardiopul­ monary syndrome (HCPS) occurs mainly in the Americas and is associated with higher mortality rates [22]. The CFR varies considerably by region, ranging from less than 1% to 15% in Asia and Europe and reaching up to 50% in the Americas [24]. Specifically, in Chile, nearly 70% of HCPS patients report occupational or peridomestic exposure to rodents or close contact with infected individuals, while 20–35% describe exposure dur­ ing recreational activities in high-risk areas [25, 26]. In Europe, 1,885 hantavirus cases were reported in 2023 (0.4 cases per 100,000 population), representing the lowest inci­ dence recorded between 2019 and 2023 [27]. In East Asia, HFRS continues to cause thousands of cases annually despite an overall declining trend [11]. In the United States (U.S), 890 hantavirus cases were reported between 1993 and 2023. In 2025, the Region of the Americas documented 229 cases and 59 deaths, corresponding to a CFR of 25.7%. In mainland France, hantavirus infection remains relatively rare, with between 14 and 320 confirmed HFRS cases reported annually since 2005, although the disease is more fre­ quent in Germany and Finland. In French Guiana, 13 confirmed hantavirus cases were identified between 2008 and May 2026 [26]. 3 Virology SARS-CoV-2 belongs to the family Coronaviridae and the order Nidovirales. It is an enveloped, single-stranded, positive-sense RNA virus composed of four major structural proteins: the envelope (E), membrane (M), nucleocapsid (N), and spike (S) proteins [9]. SARS-CoV-2 is a zoonotic virus, with evidence supporting an animal origin and subse­ quent emergence in humans. Human-to-human transmission occurs primarily through close contact via respiratory droplets and aerosols released when an infected individual coughs, sneezes, speaks, sings, or breathes deeply, particularly in crowded or poorly ven­ tilated indoor environments. Transmission may also occur indirectly through contact with contaminated surfaces followed by touching the eyes, nose, or mouth before proper Page 5 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 hand hygiene [28]. The incubation period of SARS-CoV-2 generally ranges from 2 to 7 days [9]. Notably, SARS-CoV-2 is also capable of reverse zoonotic transmission, whereby humans can transmit the virus to animals, particularly mustelid species, tigers, lions, hyenas, as well as deer and hamsters [1, 29]. Hantaviruses belong to the family Hantaviridae within the order Bunyavirales [24]. They are enveloped, spherical RNA viruses and constitute a distinct genus within the former Bunyaviridae group. Their genome consists of three segments of negative-sense, single-stranded RNA sharing conserved 3′ terminal sequences. These segments include the small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments, which encode the nucleoprotein (N), the envelope glycoproteins (Gn and Gc), and the viral RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (L protein), respectively [22]. Hantaviruses are primarily transmitted from rodents to humans [24]. However, unlike SARS-CoV-2, most hantaviruses are not transmitted from person to person. ANDV is the main hantavirus known to have this capacity, particu­ larly following close and prolonged contact with an infected individual. The first docu­ mented evidence of person-to-person transmission of ANDV was reported during an outbreak in Argentina in 1996 [30]. Subsequent cases of person-to-person transmission were reported in Argentina (1996 and 2018) and Chile (1997, 2004, and 2014), mainly in settings involving close and prolonged contact, particularly within households or dur­ ing the early prodromal phase of illness [31]. Moreover, the transmission of hantaviruses and spatiotemporal dynamics are influenced by a complex interplay of ecological factors, environmental conditions, and the behaviors of rodent reservoirs and human popula­ tions, all of which contribute to pathogen spread [4]. The incubation period of hantavi­ rus infection is generally longer than that of COVID-19 and generally ranges from 1 to 6 weeks following exposure [26]. To view a copy of this licence, visit ​h​t​t​p​:​/​/​c​r​e​a​t​i​v​e​c​o​m​m​o​n​s​.​o​r​g​/​l​i​c​e​n​s​ e​s​/​b​y​-​n​c​-​n​d​/​4​.​0​/​.​ Abstract Years after the Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, the world continues to face significant health, social, and economic challenges, while emerging and re- emerging infectious diseases remain a growing global public health concern. This trend highlights the importance of interconnected health systems and reveals both the strengths and weaknesses of global public health preparedness and response. In this context, we present a comparative analysis of the COVID-19 pandemic and the recent Andes virus outbreak, focusing on their epidemiological and virological characteristics, and discussing the effectiveness of the COVID-19 public health responses. We also explore key lessons that can be applied to future zoonotic threats in the context of rapidly changing ecosystems. The results reveal that COVID-19 and hantavirus infections share several molecular and clinical features but differ in their transmission patterns. COVID-19 spreads efficiently between humans and caused a global pandemic, whereas Hantavirus infections are mainly transmitted from rodents to humans and remain geographically localized despite a higher case fatality rate. While vaccines are available for COVID-19, none exist for Hantavirus disease. The study also highlights the value of artificial intelligence, epidemic intelligence, and the One Health approach for improving outbreak prediction, detection, and surveillance. Keywords Artificial intelligence, COVID-19, Hantavirus, One health, Public health, Zoonotic disease ​1 Introduction Emerging and re-emerging zoonotic diseases caused by both novel and known patho­ gens are increasingly recognized as a major global public health concern [1]. Zoonoses are infectious diseases that can be transmitted between animals and humans through direct or indirect contact. They are caused by a broad range of pathogens, including bac­ teria, viruses, parasites, fungi, rickettsia, chlamydia, mycoplasma, and other infectious agents. Some zoonotic pathogens have multiple animal reservoir hosts that contribute to their maintenance and transmission by supporting pathogen persistence, amplification, Page 2 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 and spillover to humans. Zoonotic infections are estimated to cause approximately 2.7 million deaths each year, underscoring their substantial impact on global health [2, 3]. Environmental modifications, including deforestation, habitat fragmentation, agri­ cultural expansion, irrigation, urbanization, and climate change disrupt ecosystems and increase contact between humans and wildlife, and have given birth to zoonotic diseases, such as malaria and Lyme disease, thereby facilitating pathogen spillover. Changes in the abundance and distribution of animal hosts can strongly influence the occurrence and transmission of zoonotic diseases in humans. For example, El Niño events in 1991–1992 and 1997–1998 in the southwestern United States (U.S) increased precipitation and veg­ etation growth, providing more food for rodents and resulting in a substantial increase in rodent populations. This ecological cascade favored hantavirus transmission among rodents and subsequently contributed to an increase in human hantavirus cases [3]. At the same time, population growth and the increasing demand for food have increased human exposure to food-borne zoonotic pathogens. Although wildlife contributes less to global food consumption than domestic livestock, the trade and consumption of wild­ life can increase opportunities for pathogens to cross species barriers. For instance, in Europe, changes in vegetation, food availability, water resources, climate, and land use can increase rodent populations and human exposure [4]. In Argentina, climate change and habitat fragmentation have been linked to recent increases in cases by favoring rodent reservoirs [5], either directly (via winter survival) or indirectly (through food lim­ itation). Studies have also shown a positive association between bank vole density and PUUV prevalence [6]. Similarly, in Brazil and the western U.S, Hantavirus occurrence has been associated with socioeconomic factors, environmental conditions, and rodent diversity [7]. Due to environment disruption, several zoonotic diseases have demon­ strated their potential to cause severe outbreaks and widespread public health impacts, including hantavirus infections, Mpox, Ebola virus disease, and Coronavirus Disease 2019 (COVID-19) [2, 3]. COVID-19, caused by SARS-CoV-2, provides a major example of a zoonotic disease with global health consequences. SARS-CoV-2 was first identified in Wuhan, China, in late 2019, where early investigations suggested an epidemiological association between the initial cases and seafood and live-animal markets. Bats are considered a likely natural reservoir of related coronaviruses, while the potential role of other animals, including pangolins, as intermediate hosts remains uncertain and continues to be investigated [8, 9]. The COVID-19 pandemic placed zoonotic diseases at the forefront of global atten­ tion, demonstrating how disruptions at the human–animal–environment interface can have profound health, social, and economic consequences [3]. It underscored the impor­ tance of understanding these interconnected systems and exposed both the strengths and limitations of global public health preparedness and response capacities [10]. Recently, the world has experienced a new hantavirus outbreak caused by Andes virus (ANDV), associated with the cruise ship MV Hondius, which departed from Ushuaia, Argentina, on April 1, 2026, and followed a South Atlantic itinerary before arriving in Cabo Verde [11, 12]. The outbreak was particularly significant not because it indicated pandemic-level transmissibility, but because it combined a severe zoonotic infection with delayed and nonspecific early symptoms, highly mobile international contacts, limited medical capacity aboard the ship, complex multijurisdictional oversight, and increased public Page 3 of 25 Madihi et al. Discover Public Health (2026) 23:1799 sensitivity to infectious disease outbreaks following the COVID-19 pandemic [13]. This raises an important question: how effective was the public health response to COVID- 19, and what lessons can be applied to the 2026 ANDV outbreak as a contemporary case study in a rapidly changing ecosystem? papers.title: Hantaviruses: Current insights, lessons from the MV Hondius outbreak, and an urgent call to action.
papers.abstract: In May 2026, a cluster of laboratory-confirmed Andes virus (ANDV) infections was reported among passengers aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship that originated in Argentina and sailed through the South Atlantic. The exposed population included individuals from 23 countries and resulted in at least 13 cases, including three deaths, representing the first ANDV outbreak with a multi-continental range and providing further evidence consistent with human-to-human transmission of ANDV. There are currently no approved treatments or vaccines for ANDV, necessitating rapid development of drug and prophylactic pipelines. The outbreak highlighted the strengths and inherent weaknesses of our existing public health preparedness infrastructure in response to emerging infectious diseases. In this Pearl, we highlight the epidemiology, molecular virology, evolution, virus-host interactions, clinical management, therapeutic development, and public health response to ANDV. We emphasize the need to expand genomic surveillance, standardize diagnostic protocols across public health laboratories, and accelerate the clinical translation of promising antiviral candidates to strengthen pandemic preparedness infrastructure for understudied and emerging infectious diseases.

PLoS Pathog 22(11): e1014756. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.ppat.1014756 Editor: Wendy Maury, University of Iowa, UNITED STATES OF AMERICA Published: November 13, 2026 This is an open access article, free of all copyright, and may be freely reproduced, distributed, transmitted, modified, built upon, or otherwise used by anyone for any lawful purpose.
