A primer on the MV Hondius outbreak Andes virus (ANDV) is the only hantavirus capable of human-to-human transmission, underscoring its potential for outbreaks that extend beyond the traditional rodent-to-human route. This significance became particularly clear in May 2026, when the World Health Organization (WHO) was notified of several cases of severe respiratory illness aboard the MV Hondius, a cruise ship carrying 147 passengers and crew from 23 countries, as it transited the South Atlantic from Argentina. Only a few days later, at least 13 cases, including three deaths, were identified and/or laboratory-confirmed, including secondary cases among contacts of the index patient [1], as well as plane passengers in close proximity to confirmed cases on a flight to South Africa [2] and a repatriation flight from Tenerife [1–6]. Contact tracing and quarantine measures were coordinated through the WHO National IHR (International Health Regulations) Focal Points and implemented across several countries, including the United Kingdom, South Africa, and the United States [2,3,7–10]. However, this outbreak is not the only recent notable case of hantaviral spread. In 2025, Betsy Arakawa, the wife of renowned actor Gene Hackman, passed away due to hantavirus infection in New Mexico, as did three people in Mammoth Lakes, California [11,12]. Hantavirus outbreaks highlight the challenge posed to public health agencies by neglected zoonotic pathogens—especially those that are ecologically complex, geographically distributed, understudied, and underfunded, yet capable of causing lethal outbreaks with little to no warning, thereby creating major public health concerns. As such, we aim to synthesize a brief primer on our current knowledge of hantaviruses and to propose areas for further research and development of emergency preparedness and capacity building within existing public health infrastructure. What we know Epidemiologic history and global burden of Hantaviruses Old World (e.g., Hantaan [HTNV], Puumala [PUUV], Dobrava, and Seoul [SEOV] virus) and New World (e.g., Sin Nombre virus [SNV], ANDV) hantaviruses are primarily carried and spread asymptomatically in rodent reservoirs. The history of hantaviruses can be traced back to the Korean War in the 1950s, when over 3,000 troops stationed along the Hantaan River fell ill with a previously unknown virus, now known as HTNV [13] (Fig 1). The first recorded outbreak of hantaviruses in the United States occurred in 1993 in the Four Corners region of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico, and Utah [14,15]. Patients passed away from fever, myalgias, thrombocytopenia, and pulmonary edema with hypotensive shock, and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) established the presence of SNV and its deer mouse reservoir. The spread of SNV was later associated with the 1991–1992 El Niño event, which caused warmer winters and increased spring rainfall, inciting a boom in the rodent population and promoting viral spread [14,15]. ANDV was first detected during a small outbreak in the Patagonia region of southern Argentina in 1995, with the first major outbreak of ANDV occurring in 2018–2019 in Epuyén, Argentina, where three distinct superspreader events occurred with no relation to inciting exposure to a rodent reservoir, confirming its ability to spread between humans [16]. A schematic showing all major hantavirus outbreaks to date. Descriptive boxes are color-coded according to the type of hantavirus (Old World or New World) responsible, with the exception of the MV Hondius outbreak, which is highlighted red for emphasis. Additionally, regions with endemic hantaviruses are colored according to whether the endemic strain is an Old World (pink) or New World (blue) hantavirus. Image created in BioRender. The global burden associated with hantaviruses reflects two divergent clinical phenotypes. Old World viruses exhibit a case fatality rate (CFR) under 1% in settings with available vaccines and supportive care, whereas New World viruses carry an estimated CFR of 30–60% [17,18]. In 2025, eight countries in the Americas reported 229 cases of hantaviral infections with a CFR of 25.7%. 1,885 cases were reported across Europe in 2023, and thousands of hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) cases have been reported annually in East Asia [7]. Molecular virology and host-virus interactions Hantaviruses (class Bunyaviricetes, order Elliovirales, family Hantaviridae) [19–21] are enveloped, negative-sense, single-stranded RNA viruses with a segmented genome (11–13 Kb) consisting of small (S), medium (M), and large (L) segments, and are associated with an envelope protein containing viral glycoproteins [22,23]. In 2024, the International Committee on Taxonomy of Viruses (ICTV) accepted a proposal to rename the class Ellioviricetes to Bunyaviricetes in RNA-dependent RNA polymerase (RdRp) phylogeny and to split the order Bunyavirales into two orders, a broader classification based on observations of increased clustering into the two distinct orders Elliovirales (including families Hantaviridae and Peribunyaviridae) and Hareavirales (including families Arenaviridae, Nairoviridae, and Phenuiviridae) [20,21,24]. Hantaviruses can be dichotomized into two classes based on their geographic distribution: Old World viruses and New World viruses (Fig 1). The key distinction between these classes is the symptoms they cause: Old World viruses cause HFRS, and New World viruses cause hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (HPS or HCPS) [17,25]. ANDV exhibits broad tropism, infecting multiple human cell types, including those of the heart, brain, and lungs, particularly lung epithelial cells. It also induces cellular injury and inflammatory responses while suppressing lipid metabolic pathways in lung epithelial cells [26]. Though less common than pulmonary or cardiac manifestations, New World hantaviruses, particularly ANDV, have also been shown to induce neurological manifestations, such as confusion, meningoencephalitis, pituitary apoplexy, and, albeit rarely, seizures, myelitis, and peripheral neuropathy [27]. Gastrointestinal symptoms, including nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, and diarrhea, have also been observed in ANDV-infected patients, both preceding and in tandem with the onset of cardiovascular symptoms [28]. However, more investigation is needed to better understand the frequency of onset, the underlying pathophysiological mechanisms, and the clinical significance of these symptoms. Since the 1950s [29,30], hantaviruses have been identified on every inhabited continent, with pathogenicity varying substantially across strains [22,23]. The differences in pathogenic mechanisms and disease outcomes among viral strains can be partly determined by viral-encoded factors, with several viral entry mechanisms elucidated in recent years. The viral M genome segment encodes glycoprotein precursors that are processed into Gn and Gc subunits, which form tetrameric complexes that help mediate cellular entry [31]. New World hantaviruses utilize protocadherin-1 (PCDH1) to directly engage viral Gn/Gc glycoprotein complexes and facilitate entry into vascular endothelial cells [32,33]. Recent investigations have elucidated the higher-order lattice architecture formed by Gn/Gc heterotetramers on the hantaviral surface, highlighting their role as the primarily necessary and sufficient proteins for viral attachment and entry [34,35]. Analysis of these surface spikes indicates that Gn/Gc complexes may serve as potential targets for antiviral immunotherapeutic interventions, including neutralizing antibodies and structure-guided immunogens [36]. Upon viral entry and genome uncoating in the host-cell cytoplasm, the negative-strand genomes are transcribed into positive-strand mRNA by the viral RdRp. Similar to some other negative-sense RNA viruses, the hantaviral RdRp can also snatch 5’-capped mRNA fragments from host-cell transcripts, allowing the virus to use these sequences as primers for transcription and replication of the viral genome [37]. The nucleocapsid protein engages the viral RdRp and host ribosomes to selectively enhance translation of viral transcripts, while also interfering with protein kinase R (PKR) dimerization and remodeling of host proteostasis pathways, blunting cell-intrinsic antiviral defenses and promoting overall immune evasion [38,39]. Additionally, pathogenic hantaviruses have been shown to dampen early type I interferon (IFN) signaling in infected endothelial cells, thus sensitizing these cells to VEGF-mediated permeability [40,41]. This mechanism may underlie the pathogenesis of HFRS and HCPS. Hantaviruses can evade immune mechanisms by using structural and nonstructural proteins, such as NSs, NP, and Gn, to block RIG-I/MDA5-TBK1 signaling, antagonize IFN induction, and induce TUFM/LC3B-mediated mitophagy to degrade MAVS, respectively [42]. Of particular concern is the capacity of these viruses to evolve, driven by the error-prone RdRP, genetic reassortment events in the L segment, and hypervariable regions in the nucleocapsid protein encoded by the S segment [43,44]. Additionally, the lack of immunity in humans increases the capacity for viral transmission and virulence. This is especially concerning given recent epidemiological trends in Argentina, which suggest that ANDV has a CFR of 34%, even higher than that of strains detected between 2019 and 2025 [45]. Phylogenetic analysis of the ANDV M-segment coding region against reference strains from NCBI revealed that the novel strain associated with the MV Hondius outbreak [46] shares 94.26% sequence identity with the ANDV reference sequence (NC_003467.2), indicating evolutionary divergence from the reference strain (Fig 2). Further comparison of this novel M-segment sequence against the NCBI Core Nucleotide Database identified closely related ANDV sequences isolated from human whole blood samples collected in Argentina (south variant) in 2018 (MN258191 and MN258192). These findings suggest that the lineage most closely related to this novel strain may have been circulating in human populations and/or reservoir hosts for nearly eight years, while gradually accumulating mutations over time. Consistent with this inference, the novel strain’s M-coding region shows the highest sequence identity with the 2018 isolates (99.0% and 98.98%, respectively). Notably, the presence of 35 nucleotide mutations but only three amino acid substitutions, two in G1 (T193A and T516I) and one in G2 (A994T), within the glycoprotein-coding regions suggests strong purifying (negative) selection, preserving critical Gn and Gc functions. Overall, these findings indicate that the functional and transmission-relevant properties of ANDV are conserved across strains despite the accumulation of silent (synonymous) mutations, underscoring the importance of sustained genomic surveillance [47]. Maximum-likelihood (ML) phylogenetic tree constructed using 1,000 ultrafast bootstrap replicates (purple circles) for 38 M-segment sequences from the genus Orthohantavirus, including 35 species from the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) RefSeq database, 2 species from GenBank (italicized), and 1 ANDV sequence (red font) obtained from a Swiss resident who had traveled on the MV Hondius cruise ship [46]. The clade containing the ANDV strain responsible for the current 2026 outbreak is highlighted in the pink box. Sequences were aligned using MAFFT v7.526, and the resulting alignment was used for ML phylogenetic tree construction in IQ-TREE. Human-to-human transmission of ANDV ANDV is unique in its capacity for human-to-human transmission, first suspected during the 1996 El Bolsón and Bariloche, Argentina, outbreaks and later confirmed at the molecular level soon after [48,49]. The 2018–2019 Epuyén outbreak subsequently provided the most extensive documentation of this transmission route, as it was notable for three distinct superspreader events without any identifiable rodent exposure [50]. Although few additional ANDV outbreaks have been recorded, the MV Hondius outbreak provided further epidemiologic observations supporting this transmission route, including secondary cases among close contacts of symptomatic passengers [51]. It should be noted that, given the limited availability of outbreak-associated sequences and lack of continuous temporal sampling, we have avoided inferring direct or continuous viral transmission. Further investigation is needed to better establish the precise mechanisms, viral tropism for upper and lower respiratory tract airway epithelium, infectiousness duration, and full spectrum of transmission routes. Clinical management and therapeutics Management of hantaviral infections primarily consists of supportive care, with early detection and extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (ECMO) in the cardiopulmonary phase remaining the most consistent determinants of survival [52,53]. Although Hantavax, an inactivated bivalent vaccine against HTNV, and a vaccine against SEOV are in active use across China and South Korea, no FDA-approved antivirals or vaccines are currently available for use in Western populations [53]. Several antiviral candidates have been investigated. Vandetanib demonstrated semi-prophylactic efficacy in Syrian hamsters [54], while ribavirin, though promising in animal models, has generally not shown robust efficacy in human clinical trials [55–58]. Additionally, polymerase-targeted antiviral strategies have been investigated in other members of Bunyaviricites, with molnupiravir showing inhibitory activity against RdRp of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus (order Hareavirales, family Nairoviridae) [59]. However, further extensive studies are required to develop and evaluate direct-acting antiviral approaches in hantaviruses. Our team has previously identified potential antiviral candidates, including favipiravir and urolithin B, that demonstrate potent in vitro activity against ANDV [26]. Favipiravir, both when used alone and in combination with ribavirin, has been shown to exhibit antiviral activity against Old World HTNV [60]. These compounds were shown to restore cellular metabolism in infected cells, thus warranting further preclinical evaluation and clinical trials. To date, most assessed antiviral candidates have only shown promise in vitro or in animal models. It should be noted, however, that one patient from the MV Hondius was treated with a combination of intravenous and oral ribavirin, favipiravir, icatibant, and baricitinib, showing complete clinical resolution of viral symptoms after 10 days [61], which highlights the potential importance of combination therapies comprising direct-acting antivirals (e.g., favipiravir) and host-targeted treatments (e.g., icatibant and baricitinib) during late stages of disease. Lessons learned and a call to action The current outbreak has highlighted the need for improved infection prevention, detection, and surveillance infrastructure worldwide. Our current public health infrastructure can be better optimized to respond rapidly to outbreaks of neglected zoonotic pathogens, such as hantaviruses. As ANDV can spread through contact with infected rodents or their urine, saliva, or feces, surveillance and early ecological warning must be prioritized, including regular monitoring of rodent reservoir populations in high-incidence areas. It has been demonstrated that a synchronous, rapid increase in rodent populations in northwestern Argentina predictably preceded an HPS outbreak in 2023 [16,62]. papers.title: Person-to-person transmission of Andes virus: a narrative review of current evidence and its clinical implications.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses constitute a group of viruses responsible for emerging zoonotic diseases primarily transmitted by rodents. Andes virus (ANDV), endemic to South America, is unique among hantaviruses because of evidence supporting limited person-to-person transmission. The aim of this narrative review is to summarize current evidence regarding interpersonal transmission of ANDV and its clinical and epidemiological implications. A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed/MEDLINE and Google Scholar including epidemiological studies, reviews, and experimental reports. Outbreaks described in Argentina and Chile, together with molecular studies and animal models, support the existence of person-to-person transmission in settings involving close and prolonged contact, particularly during the early stages of disease. Detection of viral RNA in saliva and respiratory secretions provides biological plausibility for this phenomenon. The transmissibility of ANDV has relevant implications for patient isolation, contact tracing, and epidemiological surveillance in endemic regions.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonotic pathogens mainly transmitted by rodents, and Andes virus (ANDV) is unique among them for having documented limited person‑to‑person transmission.
analysis.main_directions: The review synthesizes outbreak reports from Argentina and Chile, molecular and animal‑model findings, and detection of viral RNA in saliva and respiratory secretions to delineate transmission contexts.
analysis.current_state: Current evidence indicates that ANDV can spread between humans during close, prolonged contact, particularly in the early disease stage, influencing isolation and contact‑tracing policies.
analysis.gaps: Uncertainties remain about how often transmission occurs, which risk factors are most important, and the exact biological mechanisms, because data rely largely on case reports and limited experimental work.
analysis.future_research: Enhanced surveillance, quantitative studies of transmission dynamics, and assessment of infection‑control measures in endemic regions are required.

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses are emerging zoonoses mainly rodent‑borne, with Andes virus uniquely showing limited person‑to‑person spread. Main directions: The review compiles outbreak reports, molecular/animal data, and viral RNA detection in saliva/respiratory secretions. Current state: Evidence supports interpersonal transmission during close, prolonged contact, especially early in illness, guiding isolation and tracing. Gaps: Frequency, risk factors, and precise mechanisms remain uncertain due to reliance on case reports and limited experiments. Future research: Systematic surveillance, quantitative transmission studies, and evaluation of control interventions in endemic areas are needed.

papers.title_zh: 安第斯病毒的人际传播:当前证据的叙述性综述及其临床意义。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒是新出现的动物源性病原体,主要通过啮齿动物传播,而安第斯病毒(ANDV)在其中独特,因为已有记录显示其有限的人际传播。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 本综述综合了来自阿根廷和智利的暴发报告、分子和动物模型研究结果,以及在唾液和呼吸道分泌物中检测到的病毒RNA,以阐明传播情境。
analysis_zh.current_state: 现有证据表明,ANDV可在密切、长时间接触期间在人与人之间传播,尤其在疾病早期阶段,这对隔离和接触者追踪政策产生影响。
analysis_zh.gaps: 仍存在不确定性,包括传播频率、最重要的风险因素以及确切的生物学机制,因为数据主要依赖病例报告和有限的实验研究。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要加强监测、开展传播动力学的定量研究,并评估流行地区的感染控制措施。

papers.title: Comparative transcriptomic response of bank vole kidney and respiratory epithelial cells to distinct orthohantaviruses
papers.abstract: Orthohantaviruses are rodent-borne viruses distributed worldwide that can cause diseases of varying severity in humans following occasional aerosol transmission. While infections remain asymptomatic in their natural small-mammal reservoirs, hantaviral pathogenesis in humans is associated with an exacerbated immune response. The increasing number of outbreaks in endemic regions caused by the modification of rodent habitats due to human activities and the risks of reassortments in areas where multiple orthohantaviruses co-circulate with their animal reservoirs, are of public health concern. These challenges highlight the need to better understand how these viruses interact with host cells to spread within and between organisms, and how antiviral responses are regulated, particularly in their natural hosts. We previously showed that cellular susceptibility to orthohantaviruses depends on both cell type and virus species and correlates with cellular restrictions acting at different stages of the viral cycle. Here, we performed a comparative RNA-sequencing study and transcriptomic analysis of the cellular responses induced by three different orthohantaviruses in kidneys and respiratory tract cells derived from bank voles, the natural host of an orthohantavirus pathogenic to humans. Transcriptomic analyses revealed common as well as virus– and tissue-specific regulatory pathways that may underlie distinct infection outcomes. It highlighted the complexity of viral interactions with bank vole at a cellular level, including innate immune responses and antiviral signaling pathways.

papers.title_zh: 比较田鼠肾脏和呼吸上皮细胞对不同正汉坦病毒的转录组响应

analysis_zh.background: 正汉坦病毒es 是分布于全球的啮齿动物携带病毒,可通过偶发的气溶胶传播导致人类出现不同严重程度的疾病 (A1)。
analysis_zh.methods: 作者对来源于天然宿主——林田鼠的肾脏和呼吸道上皮细胞进行比较性RNA测序研究,以评估对三种不同 正汉坦病毒es 的细胞反应 (A6)。
analysis_zh.results: 转录组分析显示出共同的以及病毒和组织特异性的调控通路,突显先天免疫反应和抗病毒信号通路,可能是导致不同感染结果的基础 (A7; A8)。

papers.title: Assessing the performance of time series prediction models for hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome across different high-risk areas in Shaanxi Province, China.
papers.abstract: Background Hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome (HFRS) is a climate-sensitive disease. Existing forecasting models often overlook prefecture-level variations and environmental drivers. This study compares time series models incorporating environmental factors for prefecture-level HFRS prediction. Methods Monthly HFRS case counts and 14 environmental factors were collected from 2005 to 2023 in four typical prefecture-level cities, including Xi'an, Baoji, Xianyang, and Weinan. Core factors were determined via stepwise screening. We developed four time series models: univariate seasonal autoregressive integrated moving average (SARIMA) and long short-term memory (LSTM), alongside their multivariate counterparts with exogenous variables (SARIMAX and LSTMX). Specifically, multivariate models incorporated screened environmental drivers, whereas univariate models relied solely on historical epidemic data. Model robustness was further assessed by rolling-origin validation across three test years (2021-2023), in which the entire modeling pipeline was re-executed within each training window, and the sensitivity of LSTMX performance to the covariate-selection strategy was quantified. Results The predictive value of environmental covariates for HFRS forecasting varied by city and evaluation context. In Xi'an and Baoji, the multivariate LSTMX model showed lower forecasting errors (Xi'an: R 2 = 0.976, RMSE decreased from 69.246 to 17.782; Baoji: R 2 = 0.950, RMSE decreased from 6.694 to 2.805). Conversely, in Xianyang and Weinan, univariate SARIMA yielded lower errors (R 2 = 0.940 and 0.889, respectively), and incorporating covariates did not reduce forecasting errors. Rolling-origin validation across 2021-2023 yielded a consistent ranking: LSTMX had the lowest mean RMSE in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models had lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the screened covariate set was the only strategy that never caused a severe loss of accuracy, whereas including all 14 environmental variables did not reduce errors in Xianyang and Weinan. Pairwise model differences were not statistically significant after Holm correction, and the city ranking changed when the models were refitted on the monthly crude incidence-rate scale; the rankings are therefore reported descriptively and are not interpreted as evidence of regional differences in environmental effects. Conclusions No single forecasting configuration was uniformly optimal across cities: LSTMX with lagged environmental factors yielded the lowest errors in Xi'an and Baoji, whereas univariate models yielded lower errors in Xianyang and Weinan; however, these pairwise differences did not reach statistical significance after Holm correction and changed under the incidence-rate scale. When extending these models to new settings, both univariate and covariate-enhanced configurations should be compared.

analysis.summary_en: Background: HFRS is climate‑sensitive and current forecasts often miss prefecture‑level and environmental nuances. Methods: Monthly cases and 14 environmental variables (2005‑2023) from four Shaanxi cities were used; stepwise screening selected core factors; four models (SARIMA, LSTM, SARIMAX, LSTMX) were built and evaluated via rolling‑origin validation (2021‑2023). Results: In Xi'an and Baoji, LSTMX reduced RMSE dramatically (R²=0.976, RMSE 69.2→17.8; R²=0.950, RMSE 6.7→2.8); in Xianyang and Weinan, univariate SARIMA performed best (R²=0.940, 0.889) with no gain from covariates; validation confirmed these city‑specific rankings and sensitivity analysis favored screened covariates. Contribution: No single model fits all cities; LSTMX excels in two cities, univariate models in the other two, suggesting both approaches should be tested in new areas. Limitations: Model differences were not statistically significant after correction, rankings shifted with incidence‑rate scaling, and only abstract data are provided.

papers.title_zh: 评估[ PDI0000 ]在中国陕西省不同高危地区的时间序列预测模型性能

analysis_zh.background: 肾综合征出血热(肾综合征出血热)是一种气候敏感性疾病,现有预测模型常忽视地级市层面的差异和环境驱动因素。
analysis_zh.methods: 收集了2005-2023年间四个地级市(西安、宝鸡、咸阳、渭南)的月度HFRS病例数和14个环境因素;通过逐步筛选选择核心因素;构建了四个时间序列模型(SARIMA、LSTM、SARIMAX、LSTMX),多元模型使用筛选后的环境驱动因素;通过2021-2023年的滚动起点验证评估模型稳健性,在每个训练窗口重新执行整个流程。
analysis_zh.results: 环境协变量的预测价值因城市而异:在西安,LSTMX实现R2=0.976,RMSE从69.246降至17.782;在宝鸡,R2=0.950,RMSE从6.694降至2.805;在咸阳和渭南,单变量SARIMA表现更好(R2=0.940和0.889),协变量未降低误差;滚动起点验证确认LSTMX在西安和宝鸡的平均RMSE最低,而单变量模型在咸阳和渭南更优;敏感性分析显示筛选的协变量集保持了准确性,而使用全部14个变量并未改善误差。
analysis_zh.contribution: 研究表明,没有单一的预测配置在所有地区都最优:LSTMX结合滞后环境因素在西安和宝鸡产生最低误差,而单变量模型在咸阳和渭南更佳;作者建议在新环境中应用时比较单变量与协变量增强模型。

papers.title: Hantaviruses at the human-animal-environment interface: a One Health review of rodent reservoirs, surveillance, and preparedness.
papers.abstract: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome. Exposure usually arises from contact with infected rodent excreta, so prevention depends on understanding reservoir ecology, human activities, and the settings in which they intersect. This structured narrative review synthesizes evidence on host relationships, exposure, clinical and laboratory recognition, genomic investigation, and One Health surveillance across several regions. We propose three risk-proportionate tiers: baseline readiness where evidence is sparse, enhanced investigation after a credible signal, and sustained integrated surveillance where transmission is established. Five shared functions are scaled across tiers: reservoir sampling, clinical recognition and referral testing, molecular characterization, occupational and environmental assessment, and cross-sector data review. Published outbreaks in Croatia and long-running surveillance in Panama illustrate how the decision logic could be applied, while the 2026 Andes virus cruise-ship event highlights the need for diagnostics and contact management. The framework provides a practical way to plan surveillance with limited resources, but its triggers, workload, and impact remain to be evaluated prospectively.

analysis.background: Hantaviruses maintained in small mammals cause severe diseases such as hemorrhagic fever with renal syndrome and hantavirus cardiopulmonary syndrome (A1).
analysis.main_directions: The review emphasizes exposure via rodent excreta, requiring understanding of reservoir ecology and human activities (A2); it synthesizes evidence on host relationships, clinical recognition, genomics, and One Health surveillance (A3); and outlines five shared functions scaled across risk tiers (A5).
analysis.current_state: A structured narrative synthesis shows consensus on the importance of integrated surveillance and the utility of genomic investigation across regions (A3).
analysis.gaps: The proposed tiered framework has not yet been prospectively evaluated for triggers, workload, or impact (A7).
analysis.future_research: Implementation of the three risk‑proportionate tiers and assessment of their operational performance are needed to refine surveillance and preparedness (A4).

analysis.summary_en: Background: Hantaviruses in small mammals cause severe renal and cardiopulmonary syndromes (A1). Main directions: exposure via rodent excreta, host and clinical genomics, and five scalable surveillance functions (A2, A3, A5). Current state: consensus on integrated One Health surveillance and genomic tools (A3). Gaps: the tiered framework lacks prospective evaluation (A7). Future research: test and refine the three risk tiers and their operational impact (A4).

papers.title_zh: 汉坦病毒es 在人畜环境交叉口:关于啮齿动物宿主、监测与应急的 One Health 回顾。

analysis_zh.background: 汉坦病毒在小型哺乳动物中维持,可导致严重疾病,如肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征(A1)。
analysis_zh.main_directions: 该综述强调通过啮齿动物排泄物的暴露,需要了解储存宿主生态和人类活动(A2);它综合了宿主关系、临床识别、基因组学以及One Health监测的证据(A3);并概述了在不同风险层级上扩展的五项共享功能(A5)。
analysis_zh.current_state: 结构化的叙述性综合显示,各方对综合监测重要性以及跨地区基因组学研究价值达成共识(A3)。
analysis_zh.gaps: 所提出的分层框架尚未对触发条件、工作负荷或影响进行前瞻性评估(A7)。
analysis_zh.future_research: 需要实施三层风险比例分级并评估其运行绩效,以完善监测和应急准备(A4)。

papers.summary_zh: 背景：汉坦病毒在小型哺乳动物中维持,可导致严重疾病,如肾综合征出血热和汉坦病毒心肺综合征(A1)。 主要方向：该综述强调通过啮齿动物排泄物的暴露,需要了解储存宿主生态和人类活动(A2);它综合了宿主关系、临床识别、基因组学以及One Health监测的… 研究现状：结构化的叙述性综合显示,各方对综合监测重要性以及跨地区基因组学研究价值达成共识(A3)。 不足：所提出的分层框架尚未对触发条件、工作负荷或影响进行前瞻性评估(A7)。 后续研究：需要实施三层风险比例分级并评估其运行绩效,以完善监测和应急准备(A4)。

papers.title: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective.
papers.abstract: Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security.

papers.full_text: Anthropogenic drivers of recent ebola and hantavirus outbreaks: A one health perspective Zacharias Raptopoulos 1 Aristos Aristodimou 2 1 Family Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus 2 Internal Medicine Department, Limassol General Hospital, State Health Organization Services, Limassol, Cyprus Abstract Recent outbreaks of Ebola Virus Disease (EVD) and hantavirus infection have redrawn attention to the role of anthropogenic environmental change in the emergence of zoonotic diseases. Human activities, including deforestation, agricultural expansion, land-use modification and ecosystem degradation, have increasingly disrupted the interactions between wildlife reservoirs, domestic animals and humans, creating favourable conditions for pathogen spillover. In this commentary, we examine evidence linking these environmental drivers to the emergence and transmission of Ebola virus and hantaviruses, with particular emphasis on the effects of habitat alteration on wildlife ecology, viral evolution and host-pathogen interactions. We further discuss predictive models suggesting that, under current environmental and socioeconomic trajectories, the geographical risk of EVD will continue to expand. These observations underscore the urgent need to move beyond reactive outbreak response towards prevention by addressing the environmental determinants of disease emergence. We argue that the One Health framework, integrating human, animal and environmental health through coordinated multisectoral action, provides the most appropriate strategy for reducing the risk of future zoonotic outbreaks and strengthening global health security. Keywords ebola virus, hantavirus infections, ecosystem, global health, human activities, one-health-approach Graphical abstract Introduction Recent outbreaks of Ebola virus and hantavirus infections, occurring against the backdrop of accelerating anthropogenic environmental change, have renewed interest in the role of human activities in the emergence and persistence of zoonotic diseases [1], [2], [3]. Human-driven environmental changes, including climate change, land-use modification, deforestation, urbanization, and ecosystem degradation, have altered the interactions among humans, animals, and the environment, influencing the ecology and geographic distribution of infectious diseases [4], [5], [6], [7], [8], [9]. While outbreak-specific evidence for the most recent Ebola epidemic remains limited, studies of previous outbreaks caused by Zaire Ebola virus have consistently identified recurring anthropogenic and environmental factors—including population expansion, forest encroachment, climate variability, and deficiencies in water and sanitation infrastructure—that may facilitate zoonotic spillover and subsequent disease transmission [10]. Likewise, anthropogenic land-use change and agricultural expansion have been associated with an increased risk of human hantavirus infection through their effects on reservoir host ecology and opportunities for human exposure [11]. Collectively, these observations support the application of the One Health framework, which recognizes the interconnectedness of human, animal, and environmental health. Endorsed by international organizations such as the World Health Organization (WHO), the One Health approach provides a valuable framework for understanding the emergence and spread of zoonotic pathogens, including Ebola virus and hantaviruses [12]. In this commentary, we examine the potential contribution of anthropogenic environmental change to the recent Ebola virus and hantavirus outbreaks through the lens of One Health, drawing upon evidence from previous outbreaks and established ecological principles to discuss mechanisms that may underlie contemporary zoonotic emergence. Anthropogenic drivers of Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks Ebola virus disease (EVD) is caused by one of four pathogenic Ebolavirus species—Zaire, Sudan, Taï Forest and Bundibugyo—all associated with high case-fatality rates [13]. Although definitive reservoir identification remains elusive, Old World fruit bats are considered the most likely natural reservoirs or amplifying hosts [13]. Human infections typically result from zoonotic spillover following encroachment into forested habitats or contact with infected bushmeat [14]. Banik and Basu further argue that intensive farming facilitates viral mutation and reassortment, producing highly infective strains capable of efficient human-to-human transmission [14]. Moreover, approximately 31% of emerging zoonotic diseases, including Ebola virus disease, Nipah virus infection and severe acute respiratory syndrome (SARS), have been associated with land-use change driven by a 300% increase in agricultural expansion over the past 50 years [14]. Additional statistical modelling demonstrated that the probability of Ebola virus spillover in West and Central Africa increases significantly with deforestation, with every 5–10% reduction in forest cover approximately doubling the risk of outbreak occurrence [13], [14]. Hantavirus infection represents another important example of an environmentally driven zoonosis. The virus is maintained in asymptomatic rodent reservoirs and is transmitted to humans primarily through inhalation of aerosolized viral particles from contaminated rodent excreta [15]. Several studies have shown that deforestation and land-use intensification alter reservoir ecology and increase the prevalence of hantavirus infection [15]. Prist et al. describe the “dilution effect”, whereby reductions in non-reservoir species increase the relative abundance of competent reservoir hosts, thereby facilitating viral transmission [15]. Ecosystem-altering human activities not only increase opportunities for viral replication and transmission but may also influence hantavirus evolution. Holmes and Zhang argued that repeated host-switching events, rather than strict virus–host co-divergence, have been a major force shaping hantavirus evolution [16]. Habitat disturbance may further facilitate these evolutionary processes by increasing contact among reservoir species and creating greater opportunities for cross-species transmission [15]. Collectively, these examples demonstrate that anthropogenic environmental change not only increases opportunities for zoonotic spillover but also reshapes host–pathogen interactions, highlighting the need for integrated One Health strategies that address environmental degradation alongside infectious disease surveillance and preparedness. The One Health framework for preventing zoonotic disease emergence Both, EVD and hantavirus infection, have a major impact on human health and society. In addition to their high morbidity and mortality, these zoonoses impose a substantial economic burden on healthcare systems and public health infrastructure [14], [17]. Redding et al. estimated that, under current trajectories of environmental and socioeconomic change, the incidence of EVD will continue to increase [13]. More specifically, the authors predicted that by 2070 the maximum geographical area affected by EVD could expand from 3.45 million km2 to 3.80 million km2 [13]. These projections emphasize that, unless the underlying anthropogenic drivers of disease emergence are addressed, the burden of zoonotic diseases is likely to escalate in the coming decades. The era in which emerging infectious diseases could be managed solely through clinical and public health interventions has long passed. The One Health framework, endorsed by the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), recognizes the intrinsic interdependence of human, animal and environmental health and advocates an integrated, collaborative, multisectoral and transdisciplinary approach at the local, regional, national and global levels to prevent future zoonotic outbreaks [14], [17]. Importantly, responsibility for preventing emerging zoonoses should not rest exclusively with Ministries of Health but should be shared across the environmental, forestry and agricultural sectors [18]. Given the strong association between land-use change and zoonotic disease emergence, environmental policies should be regarded as an integral component of infectious disease prevention [14], [18]. Incorporating zoonotic disease risk into environmental impact assessments before large-scale deforestation, agricultural expansion or other ecosystem-altering activities could facilitate the identification of high-risk practices and inform mitigation strategies [18]. Likewise, strengthening surveillance programmes targeting wildlife reservoirs, particularly bats and rodents, together with advances in genomic surveillance, would improve the early detection of pathogens with zoonotic potential before widespread human transmission occurs [18]. Such proactive measures would shift the focus from responding to outbreaks toward preventing them by addressing their underlying anthropogenic drivers. As the recent Ebola and hantavirus outbreaks clearly demonstrate, the prevention of future pandemics depends not only on advances in medicine but also on the protection and sustainable management of the ecosystems upon which human health ultimately depends. Conclusion The recent Ebola Virus Disease and hantavirus outbreaks provide compelling evidence that anthropogenic environmental change is no longer a peripheral contributor to zoonotic disease emergence but one of its principal drivers. Deforestation, agricultural expansion and unsustainable land-use practices continue to reshape ecosystems, increase contact between humans and wildlife reservoirs, and facilitate pathogen spillover with potentially devastating public health consequences. As climate change and environmental degradation intensify, similar outbreaks are likely to become more frequent unless these upstream drivers are addressed. Future preparedness must therefore extend beyond improvements in diagnostics, therapeutics and outbreak surveillance to include policies that protect ecosystems, promote sustainable land management and integrate zoonotic disease risk into environmental decision-making. The One Health approach offers a scientifically grounded framework through which governments, public health authorities, environmental agencies and agricultural sectors can work collaboratively to mitigate the root causes of emerging infectious diseases. Ultimately, preventing the next pandemic will depend not only on advances in medicine but also on our ability to recognize that safeguarding environmental integrity is inseparable from protecting human health. The question is no longer whether anthropogenic environmental change influences the emergence of zoonotic diseases, but whether global health policy will evolve rapidly enough to address these environmental drivers before the next pandemic emerges.
